Straight X-ray of the abdomen is not used for fetal well-being assessment — it exposes the fetus to radiation and has been replaced by ultrasound for all such purposes.

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: By the first Leopold maneuver it is possible to define:
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: The first Leopold maneuver (fundal grip) palpates the uterine fundus to identify which fetal pole is there. A hard, round, ballotable mass indicates the head; a soft, irregular mass indicates the breech. By identifying what is at the fundus, the presentation at the lower pole is inferred. Position is determined by the second maneuver (lateral grip). Attitude is assessed during labour and not by the first maneuver. Fundal height measurement is a separate clinical assessment. Summary: 1st = Presentation, 2nd = Position, 3rd = Engagement, 4th = Descent and flexion.

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: By the fourth maneuver of Leopold it is possible to define: 1. Attitude of presenting part to pelvic planes  2. Weight of fetus  3. Position and presentation of fetus  4. Level of uterine fundus
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: The fourth Leopold maneuver (pelvic grip) determines the degree of descent and the attitude (flexion or extension) of the presenting part. By palpating the cephalic prominence: if it is on the same side as the small parts, the head is flexed; if on the same side as the back, the head is extended. Fetal weight is estimated from fundal height and palpation globally, not by the fourth maneuver alone. Position and presentation are determined by the first and second maneuvers. Fundal height is measured separately.

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: Engagement generally occurs: 1. In late pregnancy  2. At the beginning of the second stage of labour  3. At onset of labour  4. During descent
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: Engagement is the passage of the biparietal diameter through the pelvic inlet (station 0). In primigravidae it commonly occurs in the last few weeks before labour (late pregnancy). In multigravidae it typically occurs at or shortly after the onset of labour. By the second stage of labour, the head is already engaged and descending — engagement does not occur at this stage. Descent follows engagement, so engagement cannot occur 'during descent.'

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: Chadwick's sign is:
options: Bluish discoloration of the vestibule and anterior vaginal wall
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: Chadwick's sign (also called Jacquemier's sign) is the dusky bluish hue of the vestibule and anterior vaginal wall due to local vascular congestion, visible from around 8 weeks. Softening of the cervix is Goodell's sign. Softening of the isthmus of the uterus is Hegar's sign. Chadwick's sign is a discoloration, not a discharge.

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: During the first 5 months of pregnancy, enlargement of the mammary glands takes place due to:
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: Early breast enlargement is primarily driven by hormonal stimulation — estrogen and progesterone cause ductal proliferation and lobulo-alveolar growth, supported by prolactin and hPL. Cardiac output increases are a systemic maternal change but do not directly drive glandular growth. Capillary changes contribute to engorgement but are secondary to hormonal effects. Fat deposition plays a minor role compared to glandular proliferation.

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: The iron content in blood serum during pregnancy usually:
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: Serum iron decreases in pregnancy, particularly in the third trimester, because maternal iron demands rise steeply for fetal needs and red cell mass expansion. Without adequate supplementation, pregnancy represents an inevitable state of iron deficiency. This is reflected in lower serum ferritin and serum iron levels approaching term.

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: The conditions when the symphysis-fundal height is MORE than the period of amenorrhoea are the following EXCEPT:
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: A uterus larger than expected for gestational age (SFH > period of amenorrhoea) is seen in: polyhydramnios, multiple pregnancy, macrosomia, pelvic tumours (ovarian/fibroid enlarging the lower uterine region), concealed abruption (blood behind placenta adds to uterine size), and hydatidiform mole (rapid uterine expansion). Fetal growth retardation (IUGR) causes the uterus to be SMALLER than expected, not larger — it is associated with oligohydramnios and small-for-dates.

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: Which obstetric grip is described as: 'Done facing the patient's face; hands placed over the lower pole of the uterus with the ulnar border of the palm on the upper border of the symphysis pubis'?
options: First pelvic grip – first Leopold maneuver
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: Pawlik's grip (third Leopold maneuver) is performed with the examiner facing the patient's face. The thumb and four fingers of the right hand grasp the lower pole of the uterus with the ulnar border of the palm resting on the upper border of the symphysis pubis. Its purpose is to identify the presenting part and assess whether it is engaged or mobile. The lateral grip (2nd Leopold) palpates the sides of the uterus at the umbilical level to locate the fetal back and limbs.

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: Which obstetric grip is done with hands placed flat on both sides of the umbilicus to palpate the sides of the uterus and determine the fetal back and anterior shoulder?
options: First pelvic grip – fourth Leopold maneuver
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: The lateral (umbilical) grip is the second Leopold maneuver. The examiner places both hands flat on either side of the uterus at the level of the umbilicus and palpates to identify the smooth, firm fetal back on one side and the irregular nodular limbs on the other, establishing fetal position and the location of the anterior shoulder. Pawlik's grip (3rd) is over the lower pole above the symphysis. The fourth maneuver uses a downward-facing technique to assess descent and flexion.

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: By the third Leopold maneuver (Pawlik's grip), the fetus in the uterus is defined by:
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: The third Leopold maneuver (Pawlik's grip) grasps the lower pole of the uterus just above the symphysis pubis to identify the presenting part (head or breech) and assess whether it is engaged (fixed) or still mobile. Attitude (flexion/extension) is mainly assessed by the fourth maneuver. Position/lie is determined from the first and second maneuvers. Fetal weight cannot be determined directly from any single Leopold maneuver.

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: A woman with a regular 35-day cycle has her last menstrual period April 1–4, 1993. Her estimated due date is:
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: Naegele's rule for a standard 28-day cycle: LMP (April 1) + 9 months + 7 days = January 8, 1994. Since the cycle is 35 days (7 days longer than 28), ovulation occurred 7 days later, so add 7 days correction: January 8 + 7 = January 15, 1994. January 8 is the unadjusted 28-day answer. January 1 misses the +7 days. January 22 and 29 over-correct.

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: The pregnancy test can be positive in case of: 1. Spontaneous abortion  2. Uterine pregnancy
options: Both spontaneous abortion and uterine pregnancy
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: The urine/serum pregnancy test detects hCG. It is positive in a normal intrauterine pregnancy and can remain positive for a variable period after spontaneous abortion because hCG persists in circulation even after fetal death. Therefore test positivity is not specific for a viable ongoing intrauterine pregnancy.

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: Appropriate screening tests in an early uncomplicated pregnancy include all EXCEPT:
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: Routine booking investigations include haemoglobin/haematocrit, blood group and Rh factor, VDRL/serology, blood glucose, and cervical cytology when indicated. Repeated serial hCG measurements are NOT a routine screening test in an uncomplicated pregnancy — they are used in specific situations (suspected ectopic, monitoring molar pregnancy, or threatened miscarriage), not as a standard booking screen.

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: When more than one part of the fetus presents, it is called:
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: Compound presentation is defined as the simultaneous prolapse of more than one fetal part into the pelvis alongside the presenting part — most commonly a hand alongside the head. Face presentation is a single cephalic part with extended head. Shoulder presentation occurs in transverse lie with one presenting part. Breech is a single podalic presenting part.

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: Weakening of gastrointestinal tract motility during pregnancy is connected with an increased level of:
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: Progesterone causes smooth muscle relaxation throughout the body. In the gastrointestinal tract this reduces motility, leading to delayed gastric emptying, constipation, and heartburn in pregnancy. This is a direct smooth muscle relaxant effect of progesterone. hCG, TRF, androstenedione, and estrogens are not the primary cause of gut hypomotility in pregnancy.

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: For evaluation of fetal condition, the following investigations are used EXCEPT:
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: Ultrasound, CTG, and Doppler are all fetal surveillance/well-being assessment tools. CVS is a prenatal diagnostic procedure for genetic/chromosomal abnormalities performed in the first trimester — it is used to diagnose fetal conditions, not to monitor fetal well-being on an ongoing basis. Therefore CVS is not a fetal condition evaluation tool.

Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.question: Oxygenated blood from the placenta reaches the fetal heart through:
Pregnancy — Physiology & Diagnosis.explanation: Oxygenated blood travels from the placenta to the fetus via the umbilical vein. The pathway is: umbilical vein → ductus venosus (bypassing the liver) → inferior vena cava → right atrium → foramen ovale → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta. The IVC carries mixed blood to the right atrium but is not the vessel coming from the placenta. The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta to bypass the lungs.

Puerperium.question: The newborn is the baby just after delivery until:
Puerperium.explanation: The neonatal period extends from birth to 28 completed days (4 weeks) of life. It is subdivided into the early neonatal period (first 7 days) and the late neonatal period (7–28 days). 6 weeks corresponds to the puerperium in the mother, not the neonatal period. After 28 days the infant period begins.

Puerperium.question: The clinical features of postpartum endometritis are: 1. High fever on day 3–5 of puerperium  2. Tenderness and subinvolution of uterus  3. Pathologic lochia
Puerperium.explanation: All three are features of postpartum endometritis. Fever typically arises within the first 10 days of the puerperium, commonly around day 3–5 with endometritis (1). Uterine tenderness and subinvolution — the uterus being larger and softer than expected for the postpartum day — result from inadequate involution due to infection (2). Offensive, abnormal (pathologic) lochia reflects intrauterine infection (3).

Puerperium.question: All of the mentioned about parametritis is true EXCEPT:
options: Absence of peristalsis in severe cases
Puerperium.explanation: Parametritis (pelvic cellulitis) is characterised by constant pelvic pain and tenderness — the uterus and surrounding structures are tender on examination. A painless uterus would be incorrect. Leukocytosis, high fever with chills and rigors (especially when suppuration occurs), and absent bowel sounds from associated ileus in severe pelvic infection are all true features.

Puerperium.question: The main causative agent of postpartum mastitis is:
Puerperium.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the predominant causative organism in lactational (postpartum) mastitis, accounting for the majority of cases. It enters through nipple cracks and crannies. Treatment is with a penicillinase-resistant antibiotic (e.g., dicloxacillin, flucloxacillin) to cover S. aureus. S. epidermidis and streptococci are occasionally found but are not the main agents.

Puerperium.question: Which contraceptive method has the highest Pearl index (highest failure rate)?
Puerperium.explanation: The Pearl index measures the number of pregnancies per 100 woman-years of use (higher = less effective). The rhythm/natural method has the highest failure rate at approximately 25 pregnancies per 100 woman-years. Lactational amenorrhoea has a failure rate of approximately 2. Copper IUCDs have a rate of approximately 0.8. Combined oral pills have a rate of approximately 0.1.

Puerperium.question: Most characteristic manifestations of septic shock: 1. Hyperthermia >38°C  2. Arterial hypotension  3. Oliguria  4. Shortness of breath
Puerperium.explanation: All four are characteristic manifestations of septic shock. Fever (or hypothermia in severe cases) is part of the SIRS criteria. Arterial hypotension defines septic shock (sepsis plus organ hypoperfusion). Oliguria reflects renal hypoperfusion. Shortness of breath occurs from ARDS, a common complication. No single one of these can be excluded from the classic picture of septic shock.

Malpresentations & Malpositions.question: The most typical complications during labour in breech presentation of fetus: 1. Premature rupture of membranes  2. Prolapse of umbilical cord  3. Vaginal bleeding  4. Failure of labour
Malpresentations & Malpositions.explanation: Premature rupture of membranes is common in breech because the buttocks do not fit well into the lower segment, leading to poor cervical application. Cord prolapse is more frequent because the breech does not occlude the pelvic inlet tightly, especially in footling breech. Failure of labour can occur due to poor dilatation, inadequate descent, or complications with the after-coming head. Vaginal bleeding is not a characteristic complication of breech — it is associated with placenta praevia or abruption.

Malpresentations & Malpositions.question: The frequent complications in the second stage of labour in breech presentation are all, EXCEPT:
options: Turn of a fetus by the back facing up
Turn of a fetus by the back to the posterior
Malpresentations & Malpositions.explanation: Head entrapment is a major danger, especially with an incompletely dilated cervix or large head. A deflexed head presents a larger diameter, making delivery difficult and increasing morbidity. Persistent sacroposterior position (back to posterior) causes difficulty with the after-coming head and may require specific manoeuvres. The sacrum/back rotating to an anterior position (back facing up in the supine position) is part of the normal delivery mechanism in breech — it is favourable, not a complication.

Malpresentations & Malpositions.question: Possible causes of breech presentation: 1. Short cord  2. Contracted pelvis  3. Intrauterine death of the fetus  4. Placenta praevia
Malpresentations & Malpositions.explanation: All four are recognized causes. A short cord restricts fetal movements and prevents spontaneous cephalic version. A contracted pelvis prevents the head from engaging, so the breech remains in the lower segment. Intrauterine fetal death causes loss of muscle tone, preventing normal cephalic version. Placenta praevia occupies the lower uterine segment, blocking the head from engaging. Other important causes include prematurity (most common), uterine anomalies, polyhydramnios, multiple pregnancy, and fetal anomalies.

Malpresentations & Malpositions.question: Diagnosis of breech presentation may be done by all mentioned, EXCEPT:
Malpresentations & Malpositions.explanation: Sonography definitively confirms breech type, fetal attitude, and placental location. Vaginal examination reveals a soft mass, sacrum, ischial tuberosities, and anus without sutures or fontanelles. The third Leopold maneuver (Pawlik's grip) identifies the presenting part at the pelvic inlet — in breech, a hard ballotable head is felt at the fundus and soft mass at the lower pole. The second Leopold maneuver (lateral grip) identifies the fetal back and limbs to assess position — it does not directly confirm the presentation and so cannot diagnose breech.

Malpresentations & Malpositions.question: Fetal dangers in vaginal breech delivery are all mentioned, EXCEPT:
Malpresentations & Malpositions.explanation: Asphyxia is the most important fetal danger, caused by cord compression between the body and the pelvis and by delay in delivering the after-coming head. Haematoma (cephalhaematoma or soft tissue injury) can result from birth trauma and instrumental manipulation. Fractures of the humerus, clavicle, and femur can occur during difficult extraction. External fetal bleeding is not a characteristic complication of vaginal breech delivery — the major risks are mechanical trauma and asphyxia.

Malpresentations & Malpositions.question: Indications for caesarean delivery in breech presentation: 1. Elderly primigravida  2. Flexed fetal head  3. Dysfunctional labour  4. Big baby
Malpresentations & Malpositions.explanation: Elderly primigravida has higher risk of difficult labour and fetal compromise, making elective caesarean preferable. Dysfunctional labour in breech risks head entrapment and asphyxia, indicating caesarean. A big (macrosomic) baby increases the risk of head entrapment and birth trauma, making vaginal breech unsafe. A flexed fetal head is FAVOURABLE in breech — it is the extended/hyperextended head that is dangerous and an indication for caesarean. Other indications include fetal distress, inadequate pelvis, and footling breech.

Malpresentations & Malpositions.question: Which are the predisposing factors of breech (pelvic) presentation? 1. Multiple pregnancy  2. Oligohydramnios  3. Prematurity  4. Fetal hydrocephaly  5. Preceding labour with pelvic presentation  6. Uterine anomalies
Malpresentations & Malpositions.explanation: Prematurity (3) is the most common cause of breech — before 34 weeks the fetus has not yet undergone spontaneous version. Multiple pregnancy (1) limits space for version. Oligohydramnios (2) restricts fetal movement preventing spontaneous cephalic version. Fetal hydrocephaly (4) places the large head more comfortably in the fundus. Uterine anomalies (6) such as a bicornuate or septate uterus impede version. Preceding breech labour (5) suggests a habitual tendency, often from a uterine anomaly — this may be included clinically but the best match to the options given is 1,2,3,4,6.

Malpresentations & Malpositions.question: The Tsovyanov maneuver in footling breech presentation is started:
options: After delivery of the fetus's shoulders
When the feet have reached the pelvic floor
After birth of the fetus up to the umbilicus
Malpresentations & Malpositions.explanation: Tsovyanov II (used in footling breech) is initiated when the feet reach the pelvic floor/vulva. The operator applies resistance to prevent early foot delivery, aiming to convert the footling presentation to a complete breech configuration so the buttocks remain as the presenting part and the legs splint the body. If started after the feet are delivered or after the umbilicus, the purpose of preventing premature leg descent is defeated.

Malpresentations & Malpositions.question: Management of pregnancy and labour in transverse lie of the fetus includes: 1. Antenatal hospitalisation  2. Hospitalisation at beginning of labour  3. Amniotomy before full cervical dilatation  4. Caesarean section
Malpresentations & Malpositions.explanation: Antenatal hospitalisation (1) is recommended from 37 weeks due to the risk of cord prolapse and early membrane rupture. Hospitalisation at onset of labour (2) ensures immediate management. Caesarean section (4) is the preferred delivery method when external version fails or is contraindicated. Amniotomy before full dilatation (3) is dangerous in transverse lie because it greatly increases the risk of cord prolapse and should not be performed.

Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.question: Induction of labour should be done if the term of pregnancy is:
Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.explanation: Normal pregnancy duration is 280 days (40 weeks). Post-term pregnancy is defined as beyond 42 completed weeks (294 days). After 42 weeks, risks include placental insufficiency, meconium aspiration, fetal distress, and stillbirth — induction is recommended at or beyond this point. 285 days is approximately 40+5 weeks (still term). 287–290 days is approximately 41 weeks (late term, not yet post-term). 300 days (approximately 43 weeks) carries even higher fetal risk — waiting this long is not appropriate.

Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.question: Maternal complications of multiple pregnancy are all mentioned, EXCEPT:
Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.explanation: Pre-eclampsia is significantly more common in multiple pregnancy due to increased placental mass and higher placental hormone levels. Postpartum haemorrhage and uterine atony are common because the overdistended uterus contracts poorly after delivery. Hypotension is NOT a recognised maternal complication of multiple pregnancy — hypertensive disorders are common, not hypotension. Other maternal risks include anaemia, preterm labour, and malpresentation.

Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.question: Complications of dichorionic twins: 1. Malpresentation  2. Conjoint twin  3. Preterm labour  4. Twin transfusion syndrome
Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.explanation: Malpresentation is common in twins due to uterine overdistension. Preterm labour is the most common complication of any twin pregnancy from uterine overdistension. Conjoint (conjoined) twins occur only in monoamniotic monozygotic twins — not in dichorionic twins. Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS) occurs only in monochorionic twins due to placental vascular anastomoses — dichorionic twins have separate placentas and cannot develop TTTS.

Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.question: Possible complications of multiple pregnancy: 1. Premature or early rupture of membranes  2. Abruptio placentae  3. Malpresentation  4. Prematurity
Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.explanation: All four are recognised complications. PROM/PPROM occurs due to increased uterine tension from overdistension. Abruptio placentae can occur after delivery of the first twin due to sudden uterine decompression. Malpresentation is common from overdistension affecting lie. Prematurity is the most frequent complication — the majority of twins deliver before 37 weeks. All listed options are genuine complications of multiple pregnancy.

Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.question: Diagnosis of multiple pregnancy may be done by: 1. Maternal age  2. Fundal height larger than expected for singleton  3. Auscultation of two separate fetal heart rates  4. Abdominal palpation of excessive number of fetal parts
Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.explanation: A uterus larger than expected for gestational age is one of the earliest clinical suspicions for twins. Two fetal heart rates heard at different locations with a difference of at least 10 beats/min is strong clinical evidence. Palpation of excessive fetal parts with difficulty identifying a single fetal pole supports the diagnosis. Maternal age is only a risk factor for multiple pregnancy (especially for dizygotic twins with assisted reproduction), not a diagnostic method. Definitive diagnosis is by ultrasound.

Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.question: After what week of gestation, counting from the first day of the last normal menstruation, is the pregnancy called postmature?
Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.explanation: Post-term (postmature) pregnancy is defined as pregnancy continuing beyond 42 completed weeks (294 days) from the LMP. The EDD is 40 weeks; beyond 2 additional weeks constitutes post-term. 41 weeks is 'late term.' 43 and 44 weeks are already well within the post-term period but are not the defining cutoff.

Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.question: The first step in the assessment of prolonged (post-term) pregnancy is:
options: Determination of the true length of gestation
Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.explanation: Before labelling a pregnancy as post-term and initiating surveillance or induction, the first and most important step is to confirm the true gestational age using all available information (reliable LMP, early ultrasound dating, timing of intercourse). Many apparent post-term pregnancies are incorrectly dated. AFI, FHR assessment, and contraction stress tests are all fetal surveillance tools used after the diagnosis is confirmed.

Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.question: Prolonged pregnancy can be associated with: 1. Increased frequency of intrauterine fetal hypoxia  2. Malfunction of placenta  3. Meconium aspiration  4. Hydramnios
Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.explanation: Post-term pregnancy is associated with placental ageing and insufficiency (2), leading to progressive fetal hypoxia (1) and passage of meconium into the liquor with risk of meconium aspiration syndrome (3). Hydramnios (4) is incorrect — post-term pregnancy is associated with oligohydramnios (reduced liquor) due to diminished fetal urine output from placental insufficiency, not polyhydramnios.

Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.question: Maternal complications of multiple pregnancy include: 1. Hypertension  2. Preeclampsia  3. Postpartum haemorrhage  4. Postpartum uterine atony
Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.explanation: All four are recognised maternal complications. Preeclampsia (2) occurs approximately 3 times more frequently in twin pregnancy due to increased placental mass. Hypertension (1) is part of the same spectrum. Postpartum uterine atony (4) results from overdistension of the uterus impairing myometrial contraction, directly causing postpartum haemorrhage (3). Active management of the third stage is essential in multiple pregnancy.

Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.question: Multiple pregnancy is associated with increased probability of: 1. Maternal diabetes  2. Preeclampsia  3. Rhesus isoimmunisation  4. Premature labour
Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.explanation: Premature labour (4) is the most common complication of multiple pregnancy. Preeclampsia (2) is also significantly increased (~3×). Maternal diabetes (1) is not a recognised complication caused by multiple pregnancy. Rhesus isoimmunisation (3) is not specifically increased in twins. If forced to choose from the given options, preterm labour is the most clearly and consistently increased risk.

Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.question: The second twin is more at risk for asphyxia and stillbirth.
Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.explanation: The second twin faces approximately 50% greater risk of complications during delivery due to uterine retraction after delivery of the first twin, which reduces placental perfusion. Additional risks include cord prolapse, malpresentation requiring operative delivery, and a longer interval between births. These factors combine to increase the risk of asphyxia and perinatal death for the second twin.

Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.question: Presence of the lambda (twin peak) sign on ultrasound indicates:
Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.explanation: The lambda sign (also called the twin peak sign) is a triangular wedge of placental tissue projecting into the base of the inter-twin membrane, seen on ultrasound in the first or early second trimester. It indicates a dichorionic placenta. The T-sign (thin inter-twin membrane meeting the placenta at a right angle without a wedge) indicates monochorionic diamniotic twins.

Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.question: In multiple pregnancy there is a high probability of: 1. Premature labour  2. Anaemia  3. Increased perinatal death  4. Prolonged pregnancy  5. Malpresentation
Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.explanation: Premature labour (1), anaemia (2) due to increased iron and folate demands, and increased perinatal mortality (3) are all well-established associations of multiple pregnancy. Prolonged pregnancy (4) is not typical — twins more commonly deliver early, not post-term. Malpresentation (5) is also increased but the best-fitting option from those given that avoids including prolonged pregnancy is 1, 2, 3.

Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.question: During differential diagnosis when uterine size exceeds gestational age, consider: 1. Large but normal fetus  2. Oligohydramnios  3. Uterine leiomyoma  4. Other gynaecological neoplasms  5. Multiple pregnancy
Multiple & Prolonged Pregnancy.explanation: Causes of uterus larger than dates include: macrosomia/large fetus (1), uterine fibroids (3) and other pelvic tumours such as ovarian masses (4) that co-exist alongside or distort the uterus, and multiple pregnancy (5). Oligohydramnios (2) causes the uterus to be SMALLER than dates, not larger. Any option including oligohydramnios is incorrect.

Contraception.question: This method of contraception prevents uterine but NOT ectopic pregnancy:
Contraception.explanation: The IUCD prevents intrauterine implantation by causing a sterile endometrial inflammatory reaction. It does not prevent fertilization, so if conception occurs with an IUCD in situ, there is a higher relative chance of ectopic implantation. Combined oral contraceptives suppress ovulation, preventing both uterine and ectopic pregnancy. The rhythm method and coitus interruptus prevent sperm deposition and have no selective effect on the site of implantation. Key point: pregnancy with IUCD in situ should be assumed ectopic until proven otherwise.

Contraception.question: Choose the barrier methods of contraception: 1. Diaphragm  2. Intrauterine contraceptive device  3. Condom  4. Vaginal chemical contraceptives
Contraception.explanation: The diaphragm is a mechanical barrier placed over the cervix to prevent sperm entry. The condom prevents sperm deposition and also protects against STIs. Vaginal chemical contraceptives (spermicides) act by destroying sperm and are often used in combination with a diaphragm. The IUCD is NOT a barrier method — it acts by causing local endometrial inflammation, impairing implantation, and (for copper IUCDs) also impairing sperm motility.

Contraception.question: Which method of contraception is preferable for those who have infrequent sexual intercourse?
Contraception.explanation: Barrier methods (condom, diaphragm, spermicides) are used only at the time of intercourse, require no daily compliance, and are ideal for infrequent or irregular sexual activity. Natural (rhythm) methods require regular cycle tracking and have higher failure rates. The IUCD is a long-term continuous method more suitable for women desiring ongoing contraception. Steroidal contraceptives require daily (pill) or scheduled use and are designed for regular sexual activity.

Contraception.question: The mechanisms of contraceptive action of combined oral pills are: 1. Inhibition of ovulation  2. Aseptic endometritis  3. Increased tubal motility  4. Alteration of the cervical mucus
Contraception.explanation: Combined oral contraceptive pills act primarily by inhibiting ovulation — the combined estrogen and progestin suppress FSH and LH, preventing the LH surge and ovulation. Progestin also thickens cervical mucus, preventing sperm penetration. Aseptic endometritis is the mechanism of the IUCD, not COCs. COCs actually reduce tubal motility; they do not increase it.

Contraception.question: The excessive menstrual bleeding is a contraindication for the following method of contraception:
Contraception.explanation: Copper IUCD increases menstrual blood loss and duration of menstruation — it is contraindicated in women with menorrhagia as it worsens bleeding and may cause anaemia. Lactational amenorrhoea works by suppressing ovulation and does not affect menstrual flow. The rhythm method and coitus interruptus have no hormonal or uterine effect and do not influence bleeding pattern. Note: the levonorgestrel IUS (hormonal IUCD) actually reduces menstrual bleeding and may be therapeutic for menorrhagia.

Contraception.question: The mechanisms of contraceptive action of intrauterine contraceptive devices are: 1. Inhibition of ovulation  2. Aseptic endometritis  3. Increased tubal motility  4. Alteration of the cervical mucus
Contraception.explanation: The copper IUCD acts by causing aseptic (sterile) endometritis — a local inflammatory reaction in the endometrium with increased leukocytes and prostaglandins that prevents implantation. It also increases tubal motility, interfering with ovum transport and fertilization, and copper ions impair sperm motility and viability. Ovulation is NOT inhibited by copper IUCDs. Alteration of cervical mucus is a mechanism of progestin-based contraceptives (mini-pill, hormonal IUS), not the copper IUCD.

Contraception.question: Which method of contraception is contraindicated for nulliparous women?
Contraception.explanation: Classically, the IUCD is relatively contraindicated in nulliparous women due to increased risk of pelvic infection, potential risk of future infertility, and technical difficulty of insertion through an undilated internal os. Combined oral pills, the minipill, and condoms are all safe and commonly used in nulliparous women. Note: modern guidelines allow IUCD use in nulliparae with careful counselling, but in the classical exam context, IUCD is the contraindicated option.

Antepartum Haemorrhage.question: All of the following signs or symptoms characterise placenta praevia EXCEPT:
options: Cervical changes secondary to thinning of the lower uterine segment
Antepartum Haemorrhage.explanation: Placenta praevia classically presents with painless, bright red vaginal bleeding with a soft, non-tender, relaxed uterus. Increased uterine tone/tenderness is the hallmark of placental abruption, not praevia. Painless bleeding (a), thinning of the lower uterine segment causing cervical changes as it forms (c), and bleeding commonly beginning around 28–32 weeks (d) are all characteristic features of placenta praevia.

Antepartum Haemorrhage.question: Factors provoking anomalies of placental arrangement (placenta praevia): 1. Developmental anomalies of uterus  2. Inflammatory diseases of uterus  3. Repeated abortions  4. Myoma of uterus with subserous arrangement
Antepartum Haemorrhage.explanation: Developmental uterine anomalies (1), inflammatory uterine disease/endometritis causing defective decidua (2), and repeated abortions/curettage causing endometrial scarring (3) are all recognised risk factors for abnormal placental implantation. Subserous fibroids (4) grow outward and do not distort the endometrial cavity — they are not a risk factor. Submucous and cavity-distorting intramural fibroids would be relevant, but not subserous ones.

Antepartum Haemorrhage.question: The placement of the placenta relative to the internal os does not change during pregnancy.
Antepartum Haemorrhage.explanation: This is false. The phenomenon of 'placental migration' (a misnomer) describes the apparent upward movement of the placenta as the lower uterine segment develops and lengthens in the second and third trimesters. Most low-lying placentas identified at 17–20 weeks will no longer cover or be near the internal os at term. This is why a diagnosis of placenta praevia should not be made definitively before 28–30 weeks.

Antepartum Haemorrhage.question: Classification of placenta praevia includes: 1. Complete  2. Partial  3. Marginal  4. Low-lying placenta  5. Acute
Antepartum Haemorrhage.explanation: Placenta praevia is classified into 4 types: Type I (Low-lying) — lower edge in the lower segment not reaching the internal os; Type II (Marginal) — reaches the margin of the internal os but does not cover it; Type III (Partial/incomplete central) — partially covers the internal os; Type IV (Complete/central/total) — completely covers the internal os even after full dilatation. 'Acute' is not a recognised type of placenta praevia classification.

Antepartum Haemorrhage.question: Diagnostic methods used for premature separation of placenta (abruptio placentae): 1. Ultrasound  2. External manual examination  3. Assessment of fetal well-being  4. X-ray of pelvis
Antepartum Haemorrhage.explanation: Abruptio placentae is primarily a clinical diagnosis supported by ultrasound (which may show a retroplacental haematoma), external abdominal examination (to assess uterine consistency and tenderness), and fetal well-being assessment (CTG, Doppler). X-ray of the pelvis has no role in diagnosing placental abruption and should not be used.

Antepartum Haemorrhage.question: A woman presents in active labour with significant vaginal bleeding, is incoherent, and had a previous caesarean section. FHR is 60 bpm. The most likely diagnosis is:
Antepartum Haemorrhage.explanation: This is a classic presentation of uterine rupture: previous caesarean scar + active labour + massive haemorrhage causing maternal collapse/incoherence + severe fetal bradycardia (60 bpm) from acute fetal hypoxia. Vasa praevia causes fetal bleeding with bradycardia but not maternal shock. Placenta praevia typically presents with painless bleeding and a soft uterus, not collapse with this FHR pattern. Bloody show is minor bleeding with normal FHR.

Antepartum Haemorrhage.question: The most common cause of death in amniotic fluid embolism is:
Antepartum Haemorrhage.explanation: In amniotic fluid embolism (AFE), amniotic fluid containing thromboplastic substances and debris enters maternal circulation and causes acute pulmonary vasospasm and cardiovascular collapse. Death most commonly occurs in this immediate phase of acute respiratory and cardiac failure. If the patient survives this phase, DIC/afibrinogenaemia and its resulting haemorrhage may cause secondary death, but the primary cause is cardiorespiratory collapse.

Postpartum Haemorrhage.question: Postpartum haemorrhage could be a reasonable possibility in all of the following situations EXCEPT:
Postpartum Haemorrhage.explanation: Triplets (overdistension), long labour (myometrial fatigue), hydramnios (overdistension), and thrombocytopenia (coagulopathy) all directly predispose to PPH through uterine atony or impaired coagulation. Transverse lie by itself is not a direct cause of PPH — it necessitates operative delivery but does not inherently cause uterine atony or bleeding in the way the others do.

Postpartum Haemorrhage.question: A woman with complete placenta praevia delivered by caesarean section develops significant postpartum bleeding. The most likely cause is:
options: Placental implantation in the lower uterine segment
Postpartum Haemorrhage.explanation: In placenta praevia, the placenta is implanted in the lower uterine segment, which has poor myometrial content and contracts less effectively after delivery. The placental bed therefore fails to retract and seal the open sinuses, leading to persistent bleeding. This anatomical fact (imperfect lower segment retraction) is the primary cause of PPH in placenta praevia. DIC is more typical of abruption. Retained fragments and oxytocin failure are secondary considerations.

Postpartum Haemorrhage.question: Predisposing factors for postpartum infection include: 1. Maternal obesity  2. Maternal anaemia  3. Prolonged labour  4. Postmature pregnancy  5. Premature rupture of membranes
Postpartum Haemorrhage.explanation: Maternal anaemia (2) reduces host defence. PROM (5) allows ascending bacterial contamination. Prolonged labour (3) increases the duration of exposure and number of vaginal examinations. Maternal obesity (1) is a recognised risk factor for wound and uterine infection. Postmature pregnancy (4) is not listed among recognised predisposing factors for puerperal infection in standard texts.

Operative Obstetrics.question: The most important result of the increased number of caesarean sections being performed is:
Operative Obstetrics.explanation: The liberal use of caesarean section has primarily contributed to a reduction in perinatal mortality by preventing fetal loss from hypoxia, birth trauma, and difficult vaginal deliveries. Maternal morbidity is not reduced — operative risks increase with CS. Maternal mortality is not the primary benefit cited. Increased fetal monitoring is a contributing factor to the rising CS rate, not a result of it.

Operative Obstetrics.question: Indications for caesarean section include all of the following EXCEPT:
Operative Obstetrics.explanation: Previous caesarean section is not an absolute indication for repeat CS. VBAC (vaginal birth after caesarean) is successful in approximately 70–76% of selected cases where the prior CS was for a non-recurrent indication and the scar is sound. Failed forceps, fetal distress, and cord prolapse are all established indications requiring caesarean delivery.

Operative Obstetrics.question: Prerequisites for forceps delivery include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Vertex in the occiput anterior position
Operative Obstetrics.explanation: Forceps can be applied in non-OA positions — they are used in occipitoposterior and occipitolateral positions with rotation or after manual correction, so OA position is not an absolute prerequisite. Full cervical dilatation, empty bladder, ruptured membranes, and known position of the vertex are all essential prerequisites. Application in an unknown or unrecognised malposition leads to failed forceps and fetal injury.

Operative Obstetrics.question: A woman delivers a 4000 g infant with a midline episiotomy and suffers a third-degree tear. Which structure remains intact?
Operative Obstetrics.explanation: A third-degree perineal tear involves injury to the anal sphincter complex (external and/or internal anal sphincter) but the rectal mucosa remains intact. Rectal mucosal breach occurs only in a fourth-degree (complete/total) tear. The perineal body, muscles, and fascial layers are disrupted in a third-degree tear alongside the sphincter.

Operative Obstetrics.question: Disadvantages of a mediolateral episiotomy include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Relatively common extension through the anal sphincter
Operative Obstetrics.explanation: Extension through the anal sphincter is a risk of midline (median) episiotomy, not mediolateral. The mediolateral cut angles away from the sphincter and is specifically chosen to reduce this risk. The true disadvantages of mediolateral episiotomy include: greater difficulty of repair (compared to midline), higher risk of faulty or delayed healing, greater blood loss, occasional dyspareunia from scarring, and the risk of imperfect anatomical realignment.

Operative Obstetrics.question: Which type of perineal incision is easier to repair?
Operative Obstetrics.explanation: A surgical episiotomy produces a clean, straight incision with defined margins that can be closed layer by layer with accurate anatomical alignment. It heals better than a lacerated/irregular wound. A perineal laceration has ragged, uneven margins that are more difficult to appose accurately, increasing the risk of poor healing, haematoma, and infection.

Operative Obstetrics.question: Which procedure requires the least technical skill and poses the lowest risk for fetal loss?
Operative Obstetrics.explanation: Amnioscopy is a visual inspection of the amniotic fluid through the cervix to assess its colour (for meconium). It requires no fetal tissue or blood sampling, making it the least technically demanding and carrying the lowest procedure-related fetal loss risk. CVS has a miscarriage risk of approximately 0.5–1%. PUBS/cordocentesis requires ultrasound-guided needle insertion into the umbilical cord with higher fetal loss risk. Fetal biopsy is highly invasive.

Operative Obstetrics.question: Correct statements about obstetric risk factors include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: A woman with a prior ectopic pregnancy is at risk for another ectopic pregnancy
A grand multiparous woman is at risk for postpartum haemorrhage
The incidence of preterm delivery increases with each subsequent preterm delivery
Once a woman has had a caesarean section, all subsequent deliveries must be by caesarean section
Operative Obstetrics.explanation: The statement that all subsequent deliveries must be by CS is incorrect. VBAC (vaginal birth after caesarean) is appropriate and successful in ~70–76% of selected cases after one previous LSCS with a lower-segment transverse incision. Prior ectopic predisposes to repeat ectopic due to tubal damage. Grand multiparity predisposes to uterine atony and PPH. Prior preterm birth is the strongest predictor of recurrent preterm birth.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: Pathophysiologic consequences of preeclampsia include all of the following EXCEPT:
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: Preeclampsia is characterised by generalised vasospasm and endothelial dysfunction causing capillary leak. The net intravascular effect is volume CONTRACTION (hypovolaemia), not expansion — fluid shifts to the extravascular compartment causing oedema while the intravascular space is depleted. Decreased GFR, hyperuricaemia, oliguria, and decreased placental perfusion are all direct consequences of vasospasm in preeclampsia.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: Appropriate forms of management for the preeclamptic patient (BP 140/95 mmHg and 1+ proteinuria or greater) include all of the following EXCEPT:
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: Diuretics are NOT routine in preeclampsia management. They reduce an already contracted intravascular volume and can worsen placental perfusion. They are reserved only for complications such as pulmonary oedema. Bed rest, hospitalisation for supervision, serial ultrasound for fetal growth and AFI, and contraction stress tests for fetal surveillance are all appropriate in expectant management of preeclampsia.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: Pathogenetic mechanisms of gestosis (preeclampsia) include: 1. Hypovolaemia  2. Lack of decidualisation of the myometrial segment of spiral arteries  3. Haemorrhage and necrosis in many organs  4. Arteriolar vasospasm
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: All four are pathogenetic mechanisms. Defective spiral artery remodelling (2) — trophoblastic invasion fails to reach the myometrial segment, leaving vessels responsive to vasoconstrictors — is the key initiating event. Arteriolar vasospasm (4) is the resulting generalised vasoconstriction causing hypertension. Intravascular hypovolaemia (1) results from capillary leak. Haemorrhage and necrosis in multiple organs (3) occur in severe disease (adrenal, hepatic, cerebral).

Hypertensive Disorders.question: The hypertensive states concerned with pregnancy include all EXCEPT:
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: Pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH) encompasses conditions arising from pregnancy itself: gestational (transient) hypertension, preeclampsia, and eclampsia. Chronic hypertension is pre-existing hypertension that antedates pregnancy or is diagnosed before 20 weeks — it is not a pregnancy-induced condition and is classified separately.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: The fetal jeopardies in gestosis (preeclampsia) include all EXCEPT:
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: Preeclampsia causes uteroplacental vasospasm and insufficiency, leading to IUGR, fetal distress (hypoxia), and in severe cases fetal demise. Congenital malformations are caused by teratogens, genetic abnormalities, infections, or poorly controlled diabetes in the first trimester — not by preeclampsia. Preeclampsia does not interfere with organogenesis.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: The most common signs in gestosis (preeclampsia) include all EXCEPT:
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: The cardinal signs of preeclampsia are hypertension and proteinuria, with or without pathological oedema. Thrombocytopenia (low platelets) is a sign of severe disease and the HELLP syndrome — it reflects endothelial activation and platelet consumption, but it is not a common or routine finding in all cases of preeclampsia.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: The signs of severity of preeclampsia include all EXCEPT:
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: Severity features of preeclampsia include persistent severe hypertension (≥160/110 mmHg), cerebral/visual disturbances (scotomata, blurring, dimness), severe persistent epigastric or RUQ pain (from hepatic capsular distension), oliguria, thrombocytopenia, pulmonary oedema, and severe capillary leak causing ascites. Increased uterine contractions are not a severity criterion for preeclampsia.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: A 38-week pregnant patient is admitted with seizure, BP 240/160 mmHg, 4+ proteinuria, and unconsciousness. The diagnosis is:
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: Eclampsia is defined as the occurrence of a grand mal convulsion in a patient with preeclampsia that cannot be attributed to other causes. This patient has the full triad of severe preeclampsia (extreme hypertension + heavy proteinuria) plus a seizure and impaired consciousness — this is eclampsia. Preeclampsia by definition does NOT include seizures. Epilepsy would not explain the severe hypertension and proteinuria triad.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: HELLP syndrome signs include all EXCEPT:
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: HELLP is an acronym: H = Haemolysis, EL = Elevated Liver enzymes, LP = Low Platelets. These are the three defining laboratory components of the syndrome. IUGR is a fetal complication associated with the underlying placental insufficiency of preeclampsia/HELLP — it is not a sign or component of HELLP syndrome itself, which is a maternal laboratory syndrome.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: The main risk factor for gestosis (preeclampsia) is:
options: Age of primipara more than 35 years
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: Chronic (pre-existing) hypertension is the strongest predisposing factor for developing superimposed preeclampsia. Other risk factors include nulliparity, multiple pregnancy, pre-existing renal disease, and diabetes. Advanced maternal age is a risk factor but not the primary one. Hypotension is not a risk factor for preeclampsia.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: Preeclampsia in the multiparous patient is associated with all of the following conditions EXCEPT:
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: Multiple gestation (increased placental mass), diabetes, chronic hypertension, and glomerulonephritis (pre-existing renal disease) are all well-established conditions associated with preeclampsia, particularly in multiparous women. Hyperthyroidism is not recognised as an associated condition predisposing to preeclampsia.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: Preeclampsia management: salt intake should be restricted.
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: Salt restriction is NOT recommended in preeclampsia management. Normal salt intake is permitted. Aggressive sodium restriction could worsen the already contracted intravascular volume. Fluid management is important (avoiding overload while maintaining perfusion), but routine salt restriction is not part of standard preeclampsia management.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: Antihypertensive treatment during preeclampsia should be started when diastolic pressure increases to:
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: Antihypertensive drugs are indicated when BP reaches the severe range: systolic ≥160 mmHg and/or diastolic ≥110 mmHg. The treatment target is to bring SBP to 140–160 mmHg and DBP to 90–100 mmHg. A DBP of 90 mmHg is the diagnostic threshold, not the treatment threshold. 100 mmHg is below the Dutta-cited threshold of ≥110 for pharmacological intervention.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: The reason for visual impairment and headache in preeclampsia is:
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: Visual symptoms (blurring, scotomata, dimness, photopsia, even cortical blindness) and headache in preeclampsia are caused by vasospasm/vasoconstriction of retinal and cerebral vessels, combined with vasogenic cerebral oedema. Preeclampsia is characterised by endothelial dysfunction and generalised vasoconstriction. While retinal infarction can occur as an extreme consequence of vasospasm, the primary mechanism is vasoconstriction itself.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: Following are symptoms of preeclampsia EXCEPT:
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: Epigastric or RUQ pain (from hepatic capsular distension/subcapsular haemorrhage), blurring of vision (from retinal vasospasm and occipital oedema), and headache (from cerebral vasospasm and raised ICP) are all recognised symptoms of severe preeclampsia. Arthrosis is a degenerative joint condition completely unrelated to preeclampsia.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: The reason for upper quadrant abdominal pain during preeclampsia is:
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: RUQ/epigastric pain in preeclampsia is caused by subcapsular hepatic haemorrhage, which stretches (distends) the Glisson's capsule surrounding the liver. This is a severe feature and signals impending HELLP or liver rupture. Infarction is not the usual mechanism cited. Frank liver rupture is a catastrophic late complication — the pain mechanism leading up to it is capsular distension from subcapsular bleeding.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: Chronic hypertensive disease is the presence of hypertension antedating or before the 20th week of pregnancy and persisting beyond 42 days after delivery.
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: This is false. Chronic hypertension is defined as hypertension antedating or diagnosed before 20 weeks of pregnancy, and persisting beyond 12 weeks (3 months) postpartum — not 42 days. The 6-week (42-day) postpartum period is used for other purposes such as the definition of the puerperium.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: In which term of pregnancy do morning nausea and vomiting usually occur?
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: Morning sickness (nausea and vomiting of pregnancy) typically begins shortly after the first missed period and is most prominent between 4 and 8 weeks. It rarely persists beyond 16 weeks. Onset at 1–3 weeks is too early (before the missed period). Peak symptoms at 10–12 weeks or onset at 14–18 weeks would be atypical.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: Hyperemesis gravidarum has no negative impact on mother or fetus.
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: This is false. Hyperemesis gravidarum can cause serious maternal complications: dehydration, starvation with ketoacidosis, electrolyte imbalances, Wernicke's encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency), Mallory–Weiss tears, and in extreme cases hepatic failure, convulsions, or coma. Fetal effects include risk of low birth weight. It is not a benign condition.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: Management of severe preeclampsia includes: 1. Prevention of convulsions  2. Control of maternal blood pressure  3. Initiation of delivery  4. Use of antihypertensive drugs
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: All four are core components of severe preeclampsia management. Prevention of convulsions (1) with magnesium sulphate. Control of blood pressure (2) is a broad management goal. Antihypertensive drugs (4) — labetalol, hydralazine, or nifedipine — achieve BP control. Delivery (3) is the only definitive treatment. Each option that omits any of these four elements is incomplete.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: An early attribute of gestosis (preeclampsia): 1. Abnormal weight gain and oedema  2. Asymmetry of arterial pressure  3. Increased uric acid in serum  4. Thrombocytopenia
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: Rapid weight gain and pathological oedema (1) may be the earliest clinical evidence of developing preeclampsia. Hyperuricaemia (3) is an early biochemical marker reflecting reduced renal clearance. Asymmetric BP readings (2) reflecting vasospasm variability are an early sign. Thrombocytopenia (4) reflects endothelial damage and HELLP spectrum — it is a severity marker of established/progressive disease, not an early attribute.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: Point out the most characteristic manifestations of septic shock: 1. Hyperthermia >38°C  2. Arterial hypotension  3. Oliguria  4. Shortness of breath
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: All four are characteristic of septic (endotoxic) shock. Fever >38°C (or hypothermia <36°C) is part of the SIRS/sepsis criteria (1). Arterial hypotension is the defining feature of septic shock (2). Oliguria results from renal hypoperfusion (3). Shortness of breath/tachypnoea occurs due to ARDS and metabolic acidosis (4). Septic shock involves all organ systems.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: Cause of polyhydramnios:
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: Oesophageal atresia prevents the fetus from swallowing amniotic fluid, leading to its accumulation (polyhydramnios). Diabetes mellitus is also associated with polyhydramnios via fetal hyperglycaemia causing osmotic diuresis and increased fetal urine output. Renal agenesis (Potter sequence) causes oligohydramnios because the fetus cannot produce urine. Preeclampsia is associated with oligohydramnios from uteroplacental insufficiency, not polyhydramnios. If only one answer is accepted, oesophageal atresia is the clearest example.

Hypertensive Disorders.question: Management of pregnancy in a case with abruptio placentae (concealed, IUFD, preeclampsia) includes all EXCEPT:
Hypertensive Disorders.explanation: In placental abruption with IUFD, management is aimed at expediting delivery and managing DIC. Amniotomy relieves tension and initiates labour. Oxytocin accelerates delivery. Platelet count and coagulation profile assess DIC severity. Urinary output monitoring (target ≥30 mL/h) detects renal compromise. Intravenous heparin is NOT used — in consumptive DIC from abruption, treatment is delivery plus blood and blood product replacement, not anticoagulation.

Preterm & Abnormal Labour.question: Which symptoms are considered characteristic for premature labour? 1. Irregular pains in the lower part of the back  2. Sense of pressure in the lower part of the abdomen  3. Irregular contractions in the lower part of the abdomen  4. Change of character of vaginal discharge
Preterm & Abnormal Labour.explanation: All four are recognised symptoms of threatened preterm labour. Low backache (1) and pelvic pressure (2) reflect uterine activity and cervical changes. Irregular contractions (3) may precede regular established labour. Change in vaginal discharge (4) can indicate cervical effacement, infection, or early membrane changes. Any combination that excludes one of these is incomplete.

Preterm & Abnormal Labour.question: During premature labour before 32 weeks of gestation, corticosteroids are prescribed for:
options: Acceleration of maturation of fetal lungs
Preterm & Abnormal Labour.explanation: Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone or dexamethasone) are given to women at risk of preterm delivery before 34 weeks to accelerate fetal lung surfactant production and maturation, reducing the risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), as well as intraventricular haemorrhage and necrotising enterocolitis. They do not prevent infection (steroids may actually mask it), do not stabilise vascular membranes in this context, and tocolytics (not steroids) reduce uterine activity.

Preterm & Abnormal Labour.question: The tocolytic therapy should be stopped during which week of pregnancy?
Preterm & Abnormal Labour.explanation: Tocolysis is contraindicated beyond 34 completed weeks of gestation because the risks of prematurity at this gestation are low, and continuing to suppress labour carries no further fetal benefit while adding maternal risks. It should not be used at 36 or 38 weeks. It may still be appropriate at 30 or 32 weeks to allow time for corticosteroid effect and in-utero transfer.

Preterm & Abnormal Labour.question: The preterm labour is labour occurring before:
Preterm & Abnormal Labour.explanation: Preterm labour is defined as labour commencing before 37 completed weeks of gestation. Below 22 weeks is considered previable/abortion. 41 weeks is post-term. 12 weeks is first-trimester miscarriage territory. The defining cutoff for preterm labour is <37 weeks (and typically after 22–24 weeks of viability).

Preterm & Abnormal Labour.question: Preterm (premature) rupture of membranes is the rupture of amniotic membranes:
options: In the active phase of labour
Before complete dilatation of the cervix
Preterm & Abnormal Labour.explanation: PROM (prelabour rupture of membranes) is defined as spontaneous rupture of membranes before the onset of labour, regardless of gestational age. When it occurs before 37 weeks it is called preterm PROM (PPROM). Rupture in the active phase or simultaneously with labour onset is normal intrapartum rupture, not PROM. The distinguishing factor is timing relative to labour onset, not cervical dilatation.

Preterm & Abnormal Labour.question: What complications of the fetus can be observed in case of prolonged labour? 1. Sepsis  2. Subdural haematoma  3. Brain trauma  4. Haemorrhage
Preterm & Abnormal Labour.explanation: Prolonged labour exposes the fetus to intrauterine infection leading to neonatal sepsis (1). Prolonged mechanical compression of the fetal head against the pelvis causes intracranial stress and haemorrhage (4) and brain trauma (3) from supermoulding. Subdural haematoma (2) is a type of intracranial haemorrhage but is not specifically named in this context by Dutta — the named risks are infection, intracranial haemorrhage, and brain trauma.

Preterm & Abnormal Labour.question: Early signs of premature labour include all of the following EXCEPT:
Preterm & Abnormal Labour.explanation: Cervical dilatation to 4 cm represents active (established) labour, not an early warning sign. Increased vaginal discharge, uterine contractions, low backache, and worsening pelvic pressure are all early/prodromal symptoms that may precede established preterm labour and should prompt assessment, but they do not themselves confirm active labour.

Preterm & Abnormal Labour.question: The adequate time for cervical cerclage operation (prophylactic) is:
Preterm & Abnormal Labour.explanation: Prophylactic cervical cerclage for proven cervical incompetence is optimally performed at around 14 weeks of gestation. This timing is after the period of highest early pregnancy loss risk and before mid-trimester cervical changes typically begin. Some texts allow as early as 10 weeks. At 20 weeks cervical changes may already be occurring (rescue cerclage scenario). 28 weeks is too late for prophylactic cerclage.

Medical Disorders in Pregnancy.question: Most common cause of HIV infection in an infant is:
Medical Disorders in Pregnancy.explanation: The major route of HIV infection in infants is mother-to-child transmission (MTCT), also called perinatal transmission. This encompasses intrauterine (transplacental, ~5–10%), intrapartum (during labour and delivery — the most common period), and postnatal (breastfeeding). The overall risk without treatment is 15–45%; with ART and preventive measures this falls to <2%. Umbilical cord sepsis is bacterial, not an HIV transmission route.

Medical Disorders in Pregnancy.question: A diabetic mother will have the following complications in the fetus EXCEPT:
Medical Disorders in Pregnancy.explanation: All three listed options — hydramnios (from fetal hyperglycaemia causing osmotic diuresis and increased fetal urine), macrosomia (from fetal hyperinsulinaemia driving excessive growth), and congenital cardiac anomalies (from teratogenic hyperglycaemia during organogenesis) — are all recognised fetal complications of maternal diabetes. Therefore none is truly an 'except' and all listed options are true complications.

Medical Disorders in Pregnancy.question: The infant of a diabetic mother is at risk for all of the following EXCEPT:
Medical Disorders in Pregnancy.explanation: After delivery, the maternal glucose supply stops abruptly, but the neonate still has elevated insulin levels from chronic fetal hyperinsulinaemia. This results in NEONATAL HYPOGLYCAEMIA, not hyperglycaemia. All other options are true risks: increased perinatal mortality (uncontrolled DM), hypocalcaemia (often with hypomagnesaemia), neural tube defects (from teratogenic first-trimester hyperglycaemia), and macrosomia.

Medical Disorders in Pregnancy.question: Factors that can contribute to acute urinary tract infection during pregnancy, delivery, or puerperium include all EXCEPT:
options: Compression of the ureter by the large uterus at the pelvic brim
Decreased bladder sensitivity after epidural anaesthesia
Medical Disorders in Pregnancy.explanation: Increased urethral tone and peristalsis would promote urine flow and reduce stasis — this would be PROTECTIVE, not predisposing, to UTI. All other factors promote urinary stasis or introduce bacteria: ureteric compression by the gravid uterus (hydroureter/stasis), asymptomatic bacteriuria (progresses to pyelonephritis in 25–30% if untreated), decreased bladder sensation with epidural (urinary retention and overdistension), and catheterisation (introducing bacteria).

Medical Disorders in Pregnancy.question: Early deceleration on CTG denotes:
Medical Disorders in Pregnancy.explanation: Early decelerations are gradual, uniform decelerations that mirror uterine contractions — they begin and end with the contraction. They are caused by fetal head compression stimulating a vagal response causing transient FHR slowing. They are physiological and benign. Variable decelerations indicate cord compression. Late decelerations (beginning after the peak of the contraction) indicate placental insufficiency and fetal hypoxia/distress.

Menstrual Disorders.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with heavy, irregular menstrual bleeding for 8 months. Examination and USS are normal. Endometrial biopsy shows no pathology. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB) is a diagnosis of exclusion — abnormal uterine bleeding with no identifiable structural or systemic cause. Normal USS and biopsy with no pathology confirms DUB, most commonly due to anovulatory cycles.

Menstrual Disorders.question: The most important manifestation of myoma is:
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: The most common and significant symptom of uterine fibroid is menstrual abnormality, especially menorrhagia or metrorrhagia. Metrorrhagia (irregular intermenstrual bleeding) is particularly associated with submucous fibroids due to increased endometrial surface area, impaired uterine contractility, and vascular congestion. Amenorrhea is not a feature; fibroids cause heavy bleeding, not absent menses.

Menstrual Disorders.question: In fibroid which is not seen:
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: Fibroids typically cause heavy bleeding (menorrhagia, polymenorrhea), pelvic mass, and infertility (especially submucous and intramural types). Amenorrhea is NOT a feature — fibroids are estrogen-dependent and cause increased bleeding, not absent menses. Amenorrhea may occur after menopause or in pregnancy but is not characteristic of fibroids.

Menstrual Disorders.question: Causes of menorrhagia in fibroid are the following, EXCEPT:
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: Menorrhagia in fibroid is due to: endometrial hyperplasia (relative hyperestrogenism), increased uterine cavity size (more surface area to shed), and increased vascularity/venous congestion. Endometrial dysplasia refers to premalignant epithelial changes and is not a mechanism of fibroid-related menorrhagia.

Menstrual Disorders.question: In case of myoma predispose to menorrhagia are: 1. Inhibiting uterine contractility  2. Degeneration  3. Erosion of endometrial mucosa  4. Increased surface area of endometrium
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: All four mechanisms contribute to menorrhagia in fibroid: (1) inhibited uterine contractility prevents spiral arteriole compression; (2) degeneration causes vascular fragility; (3) erosion of endometrial mucosa especially with submucous fibroids; (4) increased endometrial surface area from enlarged cavity. Menorrhagia in fibroid is multifactorial.

Menstrual Disorders.question: The hormone responsible for a positive 'Fern test' is:
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: The Fern test examines dried cervical mucus under a microscope. Estrogen increases sodium chloride in cervical mucus, causing salt crystallization into a fern-like arborization pattern. This is maximal at the periovulatory phase (peak estrogen). Progesterone makes mucus thick and viscid, inhibiting ferning. Used for ovulation detection and diagnosis of membrane rupture.

Menstrual Disorders.question: For the first half of the menstrual cycle it is typical: 1. Proliferation of endometrium  2. Secretion of endometrium  3. Desquamation of endometrium  4. Regeneration of endometrium
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: The first half (follicular/proliferative phase) is driven by estrogen. Regeneration occurs early (basal layer rebuilds after menstruation) and proliferation follows (glandular and stromal growth). Secretion is the second half (luteal/progesterone phase). Desquamation occurs during menstruation, marking the beginning of a new cycle, not the proliferative phase.

Menstrual Disorders.question: The average length of the menstrual cycle is:
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: The average menstrual cycle length is 28 days, with a normal range of 21–35 days. The cycle comprises a variable follicular phase and a relatively constant luteal phase of ~14 days. The 28-day average assumes ovulation around day 14.

Menstrual Disorders.question: Prominent features of basal body temperature at biphasic menstrual cycle: 1. Decrease in the first phase of menstrual cycle  2. Decrease on the eve of ovulation  3. Decrease 1–3 days prior to menstruation  4. Increase in the second phase of a cycle
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: All four are characteristic of biphasic BBT: BBT is lower in the follicular phase (estrogen dominant), a slight dip occurs just before ovulation (estrogen peak), BBT rises ~0.3–0.5°C after ovulation due to progesterone (thermogenic), and falls 1–3 days before menstruation as the corpus luteum regresses and progesterone drops.

Menstrual Disorders.question: The term of the normal ovulation corresponds: 1. To the middle of the menstrual cycle  2. To day 14 in a 28-day cycle  3. To day 9 in a 26-day cycle  4. To the end of the follicular phase
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: Ovulation occurs at the middle of the cycle (1), day 14 in a 28-day cycle (2), and marks the end of the follicular phase (4). In a 26-day cycle, ovulation occurs around day 12 (not day 9) — because the luteal phase is constant at ~14 days, so ovulation = cycle length minus 14. Day 9 in a 26-day cycle is incorrect.

Menstrual Disorders.question: The establishment and maintenance of the menstrual cycle depend on:
options: A follicular phase of variable length
Progesterone synthesis by the corpus luteum
Prolactin release by the anterior pituitary
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: The fundamental requirement for the menstrual cycle is pulsatile GnRH secretion by the hypothalamus, which drives pituitary FSH/LH release and therefore ovarian function. Continuous GnRH suppresses gonadotropins. Progesterone from corpus luteum and follicular phase variability are downstream effects. Elevated prolactin actually suppresses GnRH and causes amenorrhea.

Menstrual Disorders.question: Second half of the menstrual cycle is characterized by: 1. Increase of level FSH  2. Secretion of endometrium  3. Atrophy of endometrium  4. Basal body temperature above 37°C
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: The luteal (second) phase is characterized by: secretory endometrium (progesterone from corpus luteum induces glandular secretion), BBT >37°C (progesterone is thermogenic, raises BBT 0.3–0.5°C), and a slight late-luteal FSH rise (as corpus luteum regresses and progesterone/estrogen fall, negative feedback is removed, FSH begins rising to initiate the next cycle). Endometrial atrophy occurs in hypoestrogenic states, not in the luteal phase.

Menstrual Disorders.question: The best predictor of ovulation is:
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: Ovulation occurs 24–36 hours after the onset of the LH surge, making it the best predictor. Estrogen peak triggers the LH surge (earlier event, less precise). Progesterone rise occurs after ovulation (confirms but does not predict). The FSH mid-cycle surge is minor and not used clinically to predict ovulation.

Menstrual Disorders.question: Characteristics of the first phase of ovarian cycle: 1. Formation of the mature follicle  2. Formation of the primordial follicle  3. Atresia of the follicle  4. Increase of the level of estrogen
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: The first (follicular) phase is characterized by: maturation of the dominant (Graafian) follicle under FSH stimulation, and rising estrogen from the growing follicle (causing endometrial proliferation and eventually triggering the LH surge). Primordial follicles form during fetal life, not during the menstrual cycle. Atresia is a background process, not the defining feature.

Menstrual Disorders.question: For the second phase of the ovarian cycle it is typical: 1. Atresia of the follicle  2. Formation of follicular cyst  3. Formation of the corpus luteum  4. Biosynthesis of progesterone
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: The second (luteal) phase begins after ovulation and is defined by: corpus luteum formation from the ruptured follicle, and progesterone biosynthesis (converting proliferative to secretory endometrium, raising BBT). Atresia is a non-specific background process. Follicular cyst formation is pathological, not a normal feature of the luteal phase.

Menstrual Disorders.question: The basal body temperature is based on:
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: After ovulation, the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, which has a thermogenic effect on the hypothalamus, raising BBT by ~0.3–0.5°C — producing the characteristic biphasic pattern. FSH drives follicular growth, LH triggers ovulation, and aldosterone regulates electrolytes. None of these cause the temperature rise; progesterone is responsible.

Menstrual Disorders.question: The possible aetiological factors of premenstrual syndrome are: 1. Oestrogen excess 2. Vasopressin deficiency 3. Progesterone deficiency 4. Pyridoxine deficiency
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: The postulated aetiological factors for PMS include oestrogen excess and progesterone deficiency (luteal phase hormonal imbalance), and pyridoxine deficiency (plays a role in oestrogen synthesis and production of neurotransmitters including dopamine and serotonin). Vasopressin is increased, not deficient, in PMS — elevated vasopressin contributes to fluid retention and bloating.

Menstrual Disorders.question: The signs of premenstrual syndrome are: 1. Breast tenderness 2. Weight loss 3. Abdominal bloating 4. Emotional lability
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: PMS features include breast tenderness (part of the classic description, linked to water retention), abdominal bloating (due to fluid retention in the premenstrual phase), and emotional lability (mood swings, depression, irritability). Weight loss is not a feature — weight gain of around 1 kg is typical due to fluid and sodium retention.

Menstrual Disorders.question: The possible aetiological factors of premenstrual syndrome are: 1. Oestrogen deficiency 2. Increased vasopressin 3. Increased carbohydrate 4. Increased prostaglandins
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: Increased vasopressin (along with aldosterone and prolactin) contributes to fluid retention and bloating in PMS, and also increases prostaglandin PGF2α levels. Increased carbohydrate intolerance in the luteal phase is a contributing factor. Increased systemic prostaglandins adversely affect renal function and contribute to physical symptoms. Oestrogen excess (not deficiency) is the hormonal imbalance implicated in PMS.

Menstrual Disorders.question: Treatment options for premenstrual syndrome: 1. Hysterectomy 2. Pyridoxine 3. Bilateral tubectomy 4. Selective serotonin inhibitors
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6, 100 mg daily) is used as pyridoxine deficiency is a postulated aetiological factor. SSRIs such as fluoxetine and sertraline treat both physical and behavioural symptoms with a reported 60% cure rate. Hysterectomy with removal of ovaries is the last resort; a hysterectomy conserving the ovaries may not cure the condition. Bilateral tubectomy is not a treatment for PMS.

Menstrual Disorders.question: Treatment options for premenstrual syndrome: 1. Hysterectomy 2. Pyridoxine 3. Bilateral tubectomy 4. Selective serotonin inhibitors
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: Hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy is a last resort for PMS; hysterectomy alone (conserving ovaries) may be ineffective as ovarian hormones drive the syndrome. Pyridoxine (100 mg daily) and SSRIs are standard treatments. Bilateral tubectomy is not a treatment for PMS — it is a sterilisation procedure.

Menstrual Disorders.question: Following medications can be used for the treatment of premenstrual syndrome: 1. Anxiolytics 2. Oral contraceptives 3. Progesterone 4. Estrogens
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: Anxiolytics (e.g. alprazolam 0.25 mg) provide relief from psychological symptoms. Combined oral contraceptives render cycles anovulatory and relieve symptoms. Micronised progesterone pessaries (200–400 mg daily) are used in the premenstrual phase; Mirena IUD is an effective alternative. Oestrogens are employed in some centres but are not included in the standard summary management table, and oestrogen excess is itself a postulated aetiological factor.

Menstrual Disorders.question: Following medications can be used for the treatment of premenstrual syndrome: 1. Prostaglandins 2. GnRH analogs 3. Diuretics 4. Prostaglandin inhibitors
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: GnRH analogues (e.g. goserelin, buserelin) suppress the cycle and relieve symptoms, though long-term use is limited by osteoporosis risk. Diuretics (e.g. spironolactone) help with bloating, weight gain and fluid retention. Prostaglandin inhibitors (NSAIDs such as mefenamic acid) improve both mood and physical symptoms. Prostaglandins themselves are an aetiological factor in PMS, not a treatment.

Menstrual Disorders.question: Possible reasons of secondary dysmenorrhea: 1. Appendicitis 2. Uterine fibroids 3. Adenomyosis 4. Endometriosis
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: Secondary dysmenorrhoea is associated with organic pelvic pathology. Uterine fibroids (especially submucous type) cause spasmodic dysmenorrhoea. Adenomyosis causes progressively increasing dysmenorrhoea. Endometriosis is the most common cause of secondary dysmenorrhoea. Appendicitis is a cause of acute pelvic pain but is not classified as a cause of secondary dysmenorrhoea.

Menstrual Disorders.question: Varieties of dysmenorrhea are: 1. Spasmodic 2. Membranous 3. Congestive 4. Congenital
