It occurs at genital sites (ovaries most common — chocolate cysts, uterosacral ligaments, tubes, pouch of Douglas) and extragenital sites (bowel, bladder, surgical scars, lung). It is NOT a true neoplasm, NOT painless (classically causes dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain), and NOT viral in origin.

Endometriosis.question: Symptoms of adenomyosis are: 1. Menorrhagia  2. Amenorrhea  3. Dysmenorrhea  4. Dyspareunia
Endometriosis.explanation: Adenomyosis classically presents with menorrhagia (most common, due to increased surface area and vascularity), progressive dysmenorrhea (cyclical myometrial bleeding increases prostaglandins), and deep dyspareunia (especially when co-existing with endometriosis). Amenorrhea is NOT a feature — adenomyosis causes heavy and painful menstruation, not absent menses.

Endometriosis.question: All statements about adenomyosis are true, EXCEPT:
options: Enlargement of the uterus, as a rule, is symmetrical
Enlargement of the uterus rarely exceeds 12 weeks
It is endometriosis of the uterus
Endometriosis.explanation: Adenomyosis causes symmetrical globular uterine enlargement (true), usually not exceeding 10–12 weeks size (true), and is correctly termed internal endometriosis (true). It is commonly associated with leiomyoma and endometriosis, but NOT characteristically associated with ovarian tumors.

Endometriosis.question: Hysterosalpingography is helpful for: 1. Diagnosis of subserous myoma  2. Proving fallopian tube patency  3. Diagnosis of Asherman's syndrome  4. Diagnosis of endometrial polyps
Endometriosis.explanation: HSG evaluates the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes by contrast injection. It is useful for: tubal patency (free dye spill = patent), Asherman's syndrome (filling defects from intrauterine adhesions), and endometrial polyps (filling defects in the cavity). Subserous fibroids project OUTWARD from the uterine surface — HSG only visualizes the cavity and cannot detect them.

Endometriosis.question: AFS classification of endometriosis includes:
Endometriosis.explanation: The American Fertility Society (AFS/ASRM) classification stages endometriosis into 4 stages based on location/depth of implants, adhesions, and ovarian involvement: Stage I (minimal), Stage II (mild), Stage III (moderate — small endometriomas, filmy adhesions), Stage IV (severe — large endometriomas, dense adhesions, distorted anatomy).

Endometriosis.question: Following can be used for endometriosis treatment: 1. GnRH agonists  2. Pituitary gonadotropin inhibitors  3. Antibiotics  4. Progestogens
Endometriosis.explanation: Medical treatment of endometriosis targets estrogen suppression: GnRH agonists (suppress FSH/LH → hypoestrogenic state → implant regression), pituitary gonadotropin inhibitors such as danazol (antigonadotropic, suppresses ovarian steroidogenesis), and progestogens (decidualization and atrophy of ectopic endometrium, suppress ovulation). Antibiotics have no role — endometriosis is not infectious.

Endometriosis.question: Endometriosis is a: 1. True tumor  2. Benign proliferative growth process  3. STI  4. Ectopic disposition of endometrial tissue
Endometriosis.explanation: Endometriosis is defined by ectopic endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterine cavity — it is an ectopic disposition of endometrial tissue (4) and a benign estrogen-dependent proliferative process (2). It is NOT a true neoplasm (it doesn't have neoplastic autonomy) and NOT sexually transmitted (etiology involves retrograde menstruation, lymphatic/vascular spread, coelomic metaplasia).

Endometriosis.question: All examinations are informative in diagnosis of endometriosis, EXCEPT:
Endometriosis.explanation: Laparoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosing endometriosis (direct visualization and biopsy). Ultrasound detects endometriomas (homogeneous low-level echoes). CA-125 is elevated in moderate-severe endometriosis and is a useful supportive marker and monitoring tool. α-amylase is a pancreatic/salivary enzyme with no relevance to endometriosis diagnosis.

Endometriosis.question: All symptoms could be found in endometriosis, EXCEPT:
Endometriosis.explanation: Endometriosis can cause cyclical symptoms at any site of implantation: melena/rectal bleeding around menstruation (bowel endometriosis, rectosigmoid), hematuria (bladder endometriosis), and dysuria (bladder/pelvic endometriosis). Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) implies esophageal involvement — which is not a recognized manifestation of endometriosis.

Endometriosis.question: Clinical features of endometriosis: 1. Infertility  2. Dysmenorrhoea  3. Dyskinesia  4. Dyspareunia
Endometriosis.explanation: The classic triad of endometriosis is dysmenorrhoea (progressive, severe — from cyclical ectopic bleeding and prostaglandins), dyspareunia (deep, from uterosacral ligament/pouch of Douglas involvement), and infertility (from adhesions, distorted anatomy, inflammatory mediators, ovulatory dysfunction). Dyskinesia refers to abnormal involuntary movements — it is a neurological term unrelated to endometriosis.

Endometriosis.question: Symptoms and signs of endometriosis: 1. Dysmenorrhea 2. Premenstrual spotting 3. Bleeding and pain with defecation, urination 4. During bimanual examination – pain and tenderness on uterine motion 5. All
Endometriosis.explanation: All are features of endometriosis. Dysmenorrhoea is the most common symptom (dull, grinding, or colicky pain beginning before menstruation). Premenstrual spotting is associated with anovulation, abnormal follicular development, and luteal insufficiency. Bladder involvement causes dysuria, frequency, and haematuria; rectal involvement causes painful defecation, diarrhoea, and melaena at menstruation. Bimanual examination reveals a fixed tender uterus with cervical motion tenderness, thickened nodular uterosacral ligaments, and tenderness in the lateral fornices.

Endometriosis.question: Heavy forms of endometriosis are characterized: 1. Exhausting pains 2. Bloody stool 3. Long bloody discharge 4. Infertility 5. All
Endometriosis.explanation: Heavy (Stage IV) endometriosis is characterised by all listed features. Debilitating chronic pelvic pain and severe dysmenorrhoea (grinding, colicky pain intensifying before menstruation). Bloody stool (melaena) from rectal/sigmoid involvement. Menorrhagia (long heavy discharge) as a manifestation of menstrual irregularity. Infertility (30–40% incidence) from dense peritubal and periovarian adhesions restricting reproductive organ mobility.

Endometriosis.question: Most characteristic sign of endometriosis is:
Endometriosis.explanation: Dysmenorrhoea is the most characteristic clinical feature of endometriosis — classically congestive, starting a few days before menstruation and progressively worsening. Ectopic endometrial tissue bleeds during menstruation causing inflammation and prostaglandin release. Infertility occurs in 30–40% of cases but is not the most characteristic symptom. Irregular menstrual cycle and miscarriage are not classical hallmark features.

Endometriosis.question: Endometriosis:
options: Duration as a rule without pain
Endometriosis.explanation: Endometriosis occurs in both pelvic (genital) and distant (extragenital) sites. Genital sites include ovary (most common), pouch of Douglas, uterosacral ligaments, fallopian tubes, and pelvic peritoneum. Extragenital sites include appendix, intestine, umbilicus, surgical scars, and lungs. It is not a true neoplasm. The aetiology involves retrograde menstruation, coelomic metaplasia, and immunological factors, not viral infection. Pain, especially dysmenorrhoea, is a major symptom.

Endometriosis.question: Ovarian endometriosis regards to:
Endometriosis.explanation: External endometriosis refers to endometrial tissue outside the uterus in the pelvis or other genital sites. The ovary is the most common site, forming endometriomas (chocolate cysts). Internal endometriosis (adenomyosis) refers specifically to endometrial tissue within the uterine myometrium. Extragenital endometriosis refers to sites entirely outside the genital tract (umbilicus, lung, intestine, surgical scars). Since the ovary is a genital structure, ovarian endometriosis is external, not extragenital.

Endometriosis.question: The most frequently occurring endometriosis is:
Endometriosis.explanation: The ovary is the commonest site of endometriosis, forming chocolate cysts (endometriomas). It is followed by the pouch of Douglas and uterosacral ligaments. Fallopian tube involvement is less common. Vaginal endometriosis is rare. When endometrial tissue is in the uterine myometrium it is called adenomyosis (internal endometriosis), a separate entity.

Endometriosis.question: Treatment for endometriosis is:
Endometriosis.explanation: Treatment of endometriosis includes both surgical and hormonal therapy. Surgical treatment is used for severe pain, associated infertility, large endometriomas, or failed medical therapy. Hormonal therapy (combined OC pills, progestogens, GnRH agonists, danazol) suppresses ovarian hormone production and induces atrophy of ectopic endometrium. Physiotherapy is not a standard treatment for endometriosis.

Endometriosis.question: Which of the following is NOT a synonym of endometriosis?
Endometriosis.explanation: Adenomatous hyperplasia refers to endometrial hyperplasia — a precancerous condition of the endometrium due to excess oestrogen stimulation. It is not related to ectopic endometrial tissue and is therefore not a synonym of endometriosis. Endometrioid heterotopia describes endometrial tissue outside the uterus. Adenomyosis is historically used interchangeably with internal endometriosis. Chocolate cyst of the ovary is a manifestation of ovarian endometriosis.

Endometriosis.question: Which method should be used for diagnosis of early forms of external genital endometriosis?
Endometriosis.explanation: Laparoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosing endometriosis, especially early lesions. It allows direct visualisation of pelvic endometriotic implants and biopsy for histological confirmation. Hysteroscopy examines the uterine cavity only. HSG is used for tubal patency evaluation and cannot detect early endometriotic implants. Fractional curettage is used for endometrial pathology, not endometriosis.

Endometriosis.question: The term adenomyosis is used:
options: In all cases of endometriosis irrespective of localisation
Only with focal growth of endometrial tissue in internal layer of uterus
In case of endometriosis associated with cyst development
Only in cases when invasion of myometrium is associated with muscular hyperplasia
Endometriosis.explanation: Adenomyosis (internal endometriosis) is defined as endometrial glands and stroma invading the myometrium, characteristically associated with hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the surrounding uterine muscle. It leads to an enlarged uterus, dysmenorrhoea, and menorrhagia. Myometrial invasion with surrounding muscular hyperplasia is the defining feature. Endometriosis associated with cysts refers to ovarian endometrioma, not adenomyosis.

Endometriosis.question: Definition of the term endometriosis: a) Dishormonal hyperplasia of ectopic endometrium  b) Tumor process  c) Benign growth of tissue morphologically and functionally similar to endometrium
Endometriosis.explanation: Endometriosis is hormone-dependent (ectopic endometrial tissue responds to cyclical ovarian hormones leading to proliferation and bleeding). The ectopic tissue resembles normal endometrium both structurally and functionally and undergoes cyclic changes. Endometriosis is NOT a true neoplasm — it is a benign ectopic growth, although it may form tumour-like lesions such as ovarian endometriomas.

Endometriosis.question: Obvious algomenorrhoea among patients with internal endometriosis of uterus corpus is closely connected with:
Endometriosis.explanation: In adenomyosis, the severity of algomenorrhoea (dysmenorrhoea) correlates with the extent and depth of endometriotic invasion of the myometrium. As the depth and spread of invasion increases, there is more cyclic bleeding inside the uterine muscle, increased myometrial pressure, and greater prostaglandin release, resulting in more severe pain. Age may influence incidence but does not directly determine severity.

Endometriosis.question: Evident pain is observed in all mentioned localisations of genital endometriosis, EXCEPT:
Endometriosis.explanation: Cervical endometriosis is usually painless because the cervix has fewer sensory nerve endings — it may present with postcoital bleeding or intermenstrual spotting. All other listed sites cause significant pain: the isthmico-cervical part (severe dysmenorrhoea), ovaries (chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia from endometriomas), and uterine tubes (pelvic pain and infertility from inflammation and adhesions).

Endometriosis.question: Which of the following is the localisation of internal genital endometriosis? 1. Ovary  2. Fallopian tube  3. Serosa of rectum and sigmoid colon  4. Uterosacral, round, broad ligaments
Endometriosis.explanation: Internal genital endometriosis refers specifically to adenomyosis — endometrial glands and stroma within the uterine myometrium. None of the listed structures represent internal endometriosis. The ovary and fallopian tube are sites of external genital endometriosis. The serosa of the rectum represents extragenital endometriosis. Uterosacral, round, and broad ligaments are pelvic peritoneal sites of external genital endometriosis.

Endometriosis.question: Characteristic signs of internal genital endometriosis are: 1. Development of significant pelvic adhesions  2. Development of large cysts (5–6 cm)  3. Muscular fibre atrophy surrounding endometriotic foci  4. Absence of menstrual cycle disorders
Endometriosis.explanation: None of the listed options are characteristic of adenomyosis. Significant pelvic adhesions are characteristic of external endometriosis, not adenomyosis. Large cysts occur in ovarian endometriosis. In adenomyosis the surrounding myometrial muscle undergoes hypertrophy and hyperplasia — not atrophy. Adenomyosis typically causes menorrhagia, dysmenorrhoea, and chronic pelvic pain — menstrual disorders are present, not absent.

Endometriosis.question: What is the most useful method of diagnosing endometriosis of the corpus of the uterus (adenomyosis)? 1. Hysterosalpingography  2. Ultrasound examination  3. Hysteroscopy  4. Computer tomography
Endometriosis.explanation: HSG can show contrast penetrating myometrial glands producing a honeycomb/sawtooth irregularity. Transvaginal ultrasound is the most practical first-line method showing enlarged uterus, heterogeneous myometrium, myometrial cysts, and fan-shaped shadowing. Hysteroscopy can detect openings of endometrioid tracts and strawberry-like endometrium, and excludes polyps/hyperplasia. CT lacks the resolution to visualise myometrial structural changes and is not routinely used for adenomyosis.

Endometriosis.question: The following method of examination should be done for diagnosing cervical endometriosis: 1. Colposcopy  2. Biopsy of uterine cervix  3. Hysteroscopy  4. Diagnostic curettage of cervical canal
Endometriosis.explanation: Colposcopy allows magnified visualisation of the cervix, identifying cervical endometriosis as bluish, reddish, or dark spots. Cervical biopsy provides definitive histological confirmation — demonstrating endometrial glands and stroma in cervical tissue. Hysteroscopy examines the uterine cavity and is not useful for cervical surface endometriosis. Diagnostic curettage of the cervical canal is used for endocervical pathology, not for diagnosing cervical endometriosis.

Endometriosis.question: Cervical endometriosis should be differentiated from: 1. Cervical cancer  2. Endocervicitis  3. Erythroplakia  4. Pseudoerosion
Endometriosis.explanation: Cervical endometriosis presents as bluish-red or dark haemorrhagic spots that may bleed during menstruation and must be differentiated from all four conditions. Cervical cancer: irregular/ulcerated lesions may resemble malignancy — biopsy required to exclude carcinoma. Endocervicitis: red, oedematous areas with contact bleeding. Erythroplakia: bright red patches due to epithelial thinning. Pseudoerosion (cervical ectropion): exposure of columnar epithelium producing red areas similar to endometriotic spots.

Endometriosis.question: Essential problems in treatment of patients with genital endometriosis: 1. Hormonal suppression of clinically active endometriosis  2. Cure of pelvic adhesion process  3. Normalisation of reproductive function  4. Normalisation of psycho-neurological reaction
Endometriosis.explanation: Treatment of genital endometriosis must address all four objectives. Hormonal suppression induces atrophy of ectopic endometrial tissue. Treating pelvic adhesion complications via surgical adhesiolysis and removal of endometriotic lesions. Normalisation of reproductive function addresses the 30–40% infertility rate through surgical correction, ovulation induction, or ART. Normalisation of psycho-neurological reactions addresses the psychological stress, anxiety, and depression from chronic pelvic pain and infertility.

Endometriosis.question: Cervical endometriosis occurs after:
options: Diathermocoagulation of cervix of the uterus
Endometriosis.explanation: Cervical endometriosis develops after trauma or procedures involving the cervix that allow implantation of endometrial cells on the cervical surface. After abortion: D&C causes mechanical trauma allowing endometrial cells to implant on injured cervical tissue. After diathermocoagulation: cauterisation damages cervical epithelium, and during healing endometrial tissue may implant. After HSG: endometrial cells may be displaced toward the cervical canal, and mechanical irritation facilitates implantation.

Endometriosis.question: All mentioned are characteristic for adenomyosis, EXCEPT:
options: Proportional enlargement of uterus before menstruation
Irregular enlargement of uterus before menstruation
Development of firm nodes in myometrium surrounded by capsule
Endometriosis.explanation: Encapsulated firm nodules surrounded by a capsule are typical of uterine fibroids (leiomyomas), not adenomyosis. Adenomyosis produces diffuse infiltration of the myometrium without encapsulation. Muscular hyperplasia (hypertrophy of surrounding myometrial muscle fibres) is characteristic. Proportional and irregular enlargement of the uterus before menstruation are both characteristic of adenomyosis from cyclic bleeding in ectopic tissue.

Endometriosis.question: Following clinical symptoms are characteristic for endometrioid cyst of ovary: a) Acute pain with acute abdomen syndrome  b) Progressive algomenorrhoea  c) Dysfunction of intestines and urinary bladder
options: All the mentioned symptoms are true
Endometriosis.explanation: All three symptoms may occur with ovarian endometrioid cysts. Acute pain with acute abdomen occurs when the cyst ruptures or undergoes torsion. Progressive algomenorrhoea (worsening dysmenorrhoea) is one of the most typical symptoms, from cyclic bleeding in endometriotic tissue, prostaglandin release, and adhesions. Dysfunction of intestines and urinary bladder occurs when large endometriomas or pelvic adhesions compress adjacent organs, causing painful defecation, constipation, urinary frequency, or dysuria.

Endometriosis.question: Endometrioid cyst of ovary should be differentiated from:
Endometriosis.explanation: Ovarian endometrioid cysts must be differentiated from all three conditions. Adnexitis (salpingo-oophoritis): chronic PID can present with pelvic pain, adnexal tenderness, and inflammatory mass mimicking endometrioma. Ovarian cystoma: serous or mucinous cystadenoma also presents as ovarian cystic masses. Subserous myoma: a subserous uterine fibroid projecting outward from the uterus may be mistaken for an ovarian mass during pelvic examination or imaging.

Endometriosis.question: Influence of pregnancy on endometriosis development: a) Enlargement of endometrioid heterotopia during first 2–3 months, after which regression  b) Greater regression during postpartum period among lactating women  c) Activation of endometriosis throughout all period of pregnancy
Endometriosis.explanation: In early pregnancy, decidual changes in endometriotic implants may cause temporary enlargement in the first 2–3 months. Later, due to high progesterone levels and anovulation, endometriotic tissue undergoes atrophy and regression. During lactation, prolactin suppresses ovulation and oestrogen production, further promoting regression. Activation of endometriosis throughout the entire pregnancy is incorrect — pregnancy generally suppresses endometriosis.

Endometriosis.question: Characteristic clinical signs of internal endometriosis of the uterus are: 1. Infertility  2. Spotting before and after menstruation  3. Hyperpolymenorrhoea  4. Secondary anaemia
Endometriosis.explanation: All four features are characteristic of adenomyosis (internal endometriosis). Infertility: adenomyosis can interfere with implantation and uterine contractility. Spotting before and after menstruation: ectopic endometrial tissue within the myometrium bleeds cyclically. Hyperpolymenorrhoea: adenomyosis commonly causes heavy and prolonged menstrual bleeding from increased endometrial surface area and myometrial dysfunction. Secondary anaemia: chronic heavy menstrual blood loss leads to iron-deficiency anaemia.

Endometriosis.question: At what time is it normal to perform daily measurement of basal body temperature?
options: In the morning, just after waking up
In the morning, after defecation and urination
Endometriosis.explanation: Basal body temperature (BBT) must be measured immediately after waking, before getting out of bed, before eating, urinating, or any activity. This ensures the reading reflects the true basal metabolic state. Physical activity such as walking to the bathroom can increase temperature and make the reading inaccurate. Body temperature varies throughout the day due to activity, food intake, and circadian rhythm. BBT rises by ~0.3–0.5°C after ovulation due to progesterone.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: What is the cause for luteal phase defect?
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Luteal phase defect (LPD) is caused by inadequate progesterone secretion from the corpus luteum. Progesterone is essential for transforming proliferative endometrium to secretory endometrium and preparing for implantation. Inadequate LH support leads to poor corpus luteum function, insufficient progesterone, inadequate endometrial maturation, and results in infertility or early pregnancy loss.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: Post coital test detects all of the following, except:
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: The post-coital test (Sims-Huhner test) assesses sperm-cervical mucus interaction. It evaluates cervical factor abnormality (mucus quality, spinnbarkeit, ferning), sperm presence/count in mucus, and sperm motility/abnormality. It CANNOT detect fallopian tube blockage — tubal patency requires HSG, sonosalpingography, or laparoscopic chromotubation.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: Post coital test (PCT) is done for:
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: The PCT (Sims-Huhner test) is performed 6-12 hours after intercourse around ovulation to assess cervical receptivity — quality/quantity of cervical mucus, presence of motile sperm, and sperm-mucus interaction. Tubal patency requires HSG or laparoscopy. Absolute sperm count and semen volume are assessed by semen analysis.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: In vitro fertilization is indicated in:
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: IVF was originally developed for bilateral tubal damage/blockage, as it bypasses the fallopian tubes entirely by direct oocyte retrieval and embryo transfer to the uterus. Uterine dysfunction may require surrogacy. Severe ovarian failure requires donor oocytes. PID itself is not an indication — only the resulting tubal damage becomes an indication.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: Lady with infertility with bilateral tubal block at cornu – method of management is:
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Bilateral cornual (proximal) tubal block makes natural fertilization impossible. IVF is the definitive treatment as it completely bypasses the fallopian tubes. Laparoscopy/hysteroscopy are mainly diagnostic. Hydrotubation is outdated and ineffective for true anatomical block. Tuboplasty has poor success rates for bilateral proximal disease and high ectopic pregnancy risk.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: Possible investigation to assess tubal patency:
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Laparoscopic chromotubation is the gold standard for tubal patency — methylene blue dye is injected through the cervix and direct visualization confirms dye spill from fimbrial ends. It also detects peritubal adhesions and endometriosis. Colposcopy is for cervix only. Hysteroscopy visualizes the uterine cavity. Laparotomy is not a routine diagnostic procedure.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: Appropriate therapy for endocrine infertility includes: 1. Clomiphene citrate  2. Human chorionic gonadotropin  3. Postovulatory progesterone supplementation  4. Prolactin using
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Appropriate therapies for endocrine infertility: clomiphene (SERM, first-line for anovulation, blocks estrogen feedback to increase FSH/LH), hCG (mimics LH surge to trigger ovulation), and postovulatory progesterone (luteal phase support). Prolactin itself is NOT a treatment — hyperprolactinemia causes anovulation and is treated with dopamine agonists (bromocriptine, cabergoline).

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: All are used in treatment of infertility, except:
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: FSH (stimulates follicular growth in ovulation induction), pulsatile GnRH (for hypothalamic amenorrhea), and clomiphene (first-line for anovulatory infertility) are all used. Prolactin is NOT used — elevated prolactin inhibits GnRH and causes anovulation. Treatment of hyperprolactinemia uses dopamine agonists to reduce prolactin levels.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: Absolute inability to conceive for one or more reasons is:
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Sterility is defined as absolute inability to conceive due to irreversible causes (absent uterus, bilateral absent ovaries, bilateral tubal block, azoospermia). Infertility is failure to conceive after 1 year of regular unprotected intercourse — conception may still be possible with treatment, so it is not absolute. Disability and inability are not standard reproductive medicine terms.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: Uterine causes of infertility are: 1. Asherman's syndrome  2. Peritubal adhesions  3. PCOD  4. Myoma
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Uterine causes of infertility: Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine adhesions causing endometrial destruction and impaired implantation) and myoma (especially submucous and cavity-distorting intramural fibroids, interfering with implantation and sperm transport). Peritubal adhesions are a tubal factor. PCOD is an ovarian factor causing anovulation.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: The term 'infertile marriage' means: 1. Conception inability in the couple 2. Carriage inability in women 3. Both
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Infertility is defined as the failure of a couple to achieve pregnancy (conception) after one year of regular unprotected intercourse. The inability to carry a pregnancy (habitual abortion) is a separate entity — certain uterine causes (incompetent os, malformations) cause habitual abortion more than infertility. The term 'infertile marriage' therefore refers specifically to conception inability.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: Marriage is considered infertile if pregnancy doesn't occur in regular sexual life without using contraceptives during:
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: A couple is considered infertile after 1 year of regular unprotected intercourse without conception. Approximately 80% of normal couples conceive within 1 year — about 50% by 3 months and 75% by 6 months. Investigations are initiated after this 1-year period.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: Causes of infertility in married woman: 1. Inflammatory diseases of the female genital organs 2. Infantilism and hypoplasia of genital organs 3. Common exhausting diseases and intoxication 4. All the mentioned
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: All listed factors cause infertility. PID and genital tuberculosis cause tubal damage, adhesions, and blockage. Infantilism and hypoplasia (underdeveloped or rudimentary organs including a small hypoplastic uterus) lead to menstrual disorders and infertility. Systemic diseases (tuberculosis, diabetes, renal disease), malnutrition, anaemia, and intoxication (tobacco, alcohol, drugs, chemicals) disrupt hormonal and reproductive function.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: In infertility, it's preferable to carry out hysterosalpingography on the:
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: HSG in infertility is best performed at the 9th or 10th day of the cycle (the pre-ovulatory phase). This timing ensures a fertilized ovum cannot be disturbed, avoids risks of oil/gas embolism and induction of pelvic endometriosis associated with premenstrual or post-ovulatory timing, and avoids thick premenstrual endometrium that may obstruct dye flow at the cornual end of the tubes.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: Postcoital test is used to assess: 1. Cervical factor 2. Vaginal factor 3. Uterine factor 4. None
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: The postcoital test (Sims' or Huhner's test) primarily assesses the cervical factor in infertility. It evaluates sperm-cervical mucus interaction, the oestrogenic effect on mucus (which should be thin and profuse at ovulation), the presence of antisperm antibodies causing sperm immobilisation, and cervicitis (leucocytes in mucus). It also assesses whether the cervix is correctly positioned to reach the seminal pool.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: After ovulation the ovum keeps the capability of fertilization during:
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: After ovulation, the ovum is potentially fertilisable for approximately 12 hours, rarely up to 24 hours. Beyond this window, it degenerates in the fallopian tube without leaving any trace. The ovum's survival period is shorter than that of a spermatozoon (~24 hours). Therefore coitus must occur within the 24-hour window surrounding ovulation for fertilisation to occur.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: Spermatozoa penetrate into the uterine tubes and the abdominal cavity after coitus within:
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Spermatozoa typically reach the uterine tubes and abdominal cavity within 30–60 minutes of coitus, covering ~20 cm from ejaculation site to the ampulla. During ovulation, increased uterine peristalsis can facilitate more rapid transport. The vaginal environment (pH 4.5) is lethal to sperm within 2–4 hours, while the alkaline cervical medium supports their migration against the ciliary current.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: In fertile period: 1. Estrogen decreases 2. Estrogen increases 3. Progesterone increases 4. Progesterone decreases
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: During the fertile period (surrounding ovulation), oestrogen (oestradiol) rises significantly, peaking at 300–600 mcg about 48 hours before ovulation (rising from 100–200 pg/mL in the follicular phase to 300–500 pg/mL at ovulation). This oestrogen surge triggers the LH surge and renders cervical mucus thin, profuse, and alkaline for sperm penetration. Progesterone remains low (~1 ng/mL) until after ovulation when the corpus luteum forms.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: Point out a postcoital oral contraceptive:
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Postinor contains levonorgestrel, a progestin used for emergency (postcoital) contraception. It works by inhibiting or delaying ovulation, altering cervical mucus, and preventing fertilisation and implantation. It is taken within 72 hours of intercourse. Emergency contraceptive options include levonorgestrel (Postinor), ulipristal acetate, the combined oestrogen-progestin Yuzpe method, and copper IUCD (most effective if within 5 days). Denovis and Gynophase are combined oral contraceptive pills used for regular contraception, not specifically for postcoital use.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: Infertility refers to couple's inability to conception. It can also include:
options: Women's disability for carrying of pregnancy
Both conception inability and carrying inability
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Infertility refers to the inability of a couple to conceive after 1 year of regular unprotected sexual intercourse. This problem may arise due to female factors (~40%: ovulatory disorders, tubal blockage, uterine abnormalities, endometriosis), male factors (~40%: low sperm count, poor motility, abnormal morphology), combined causes (~10–20%), or unexplained infertility. Therefore infertility can involve both conception inability and carriage inability in a broader clinical sense.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: The spermatozoon penetrates into the uterine cavity in ........... after intercourse:
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: After ejaculation in the vagina, spermatozoa rapidly migrate through the cervix and uterine cavity due to sperm motility, uterine contractions stimulated by prostaglandins in semen, and cervical mucus channels (especially during ovulation). Sperm can reach the uterine cavity within about 5 minutes after intercourse. Note the distinction: sperm reach the uterine cavity at ~5 minutes, but reach the fallopian tubes and abdominal cavity at 30–60 minutes.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: The spermatozoon can retain the moving ability in the crypts of the cervical canal during:
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: After ejaculation, spermatozoa stored in the crypts of the cervical canal can remain viable and motile for 3–5 days. The cervical mucus (especially during the ovulatory phase) provides nutrients, protection from vaginal acidity, and channels that allow sperm survival. Under favourable conditions, sperm retain motility and fertilising ability for about 3–5 days in the female genital tract. This is distinct from their fertilising capacity once in the uterus and tubes, which is considered 24–48 hours. Ovum survival after ovulation is ~12–24 hours.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: After getting into the uterus and tubes, the spermatozoa retain the possibility of insemination during:
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: After spermatozoa enter the uterus and fallopian tubes, they undergo capacitation — a physiological process enabling the acrosome reaction necessary for ovum penetration. Once capacitated, sperm have a limited window of optimal fertilising ability of approximately 24–48 hours. While sperm may biologically survive in cervical crypts for up to 3–5 days, their effective fertilising capacity after reaching the uterus and tubes is 24–48 hours. This distinction between biological survival (3–5 days in cervical crypts) and fertilising capacity (24–48 hours after reaching the tubes) is important for exam purposes.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: During the revelation of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome it is necessary to: 1. Stop the use of medicine that stimulates ovulation  2. Ensure physical and psycho-emotional rest  3. Replace the medicine stimulating ovulation  4. Urgent laparotomy, removal or resection of abnormal ovary
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) is a complication of ovulation-induction therapy (e.g. gonadotropins, clomiphene). Management is mainly conservative in mild-moderate cases. The first step is to discontinue ovulation-stimulating drugs to prevent further ovarian enlargement. Bed rest, monitoring, fluid balance, and supportive care help reduce complications such as ovarian torsion and fluid imbalance. Replacing stimulating drugs is incorrect — they must be stopped, not substituted. Urgent laparotomy is not standard treatment for OHSS; surgery is only considered in rare acute complications such as ovarian torsion or rupture.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: The most common reasons of tubal infertility are: 1. Non-specific inflammatory diseases of uterine adnexa  2. Specific inflammatory diseases of uterine adnexa  3. Endometriosis of uterine tubes  4. Uterine tube malformations
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Tubal infertility results from damage or obstruction of the fallopian tubes. Non-specific inflammatory disease (PID from Chlamydia, Gonococcus, or mixed flora) is the most common cause, leading to adhesions, fibrosis, and tubal obstruction. Specific inflammatory diseases such as genital tuberculosis cause severe tubal damage and blockage. Endometriosis can cause adhesions and distortion of tubal anatomy, impairing ovum pickup and transport. Congenital uterine tube malformations are rare and therefore not a common cause. Tubal/peritoneal factors account for ~30–40% of female infertility.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: The most informative method of diagnosing minor forms of endometriosis is:
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Laparoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis of endometriosis, especially minor forms (minimal or mild). Small lesions, implants, or adhesions are not visible on imaging studies. Laparoscopy allows direct visualisation of pelvic organs and endometriotic implants, and biopsy can be taken for histological confirmation. Hysterosalpingography assesses uterine cavity and tubal patency but cannot reliably detect small endometriotic lesions. Hysteroscopy allows visualisation of the uterine cavity only; endometriosis occurs outside the cavity. Kimopertubation evaluates tubal patency by passing gas but does not detect endometriotic implants.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: Surgical treatment of tubal infertility is indicated: 1. In all cases if mechanical tubal infertility has been detected  2. In case of often recurring inflammatory processes in uterine adnexa  3. In case of detection of obstruction of one of the uterine tubes  4. In case of no effect from conservative treatment and persistent desire of the woman to have children
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Surgical treatment for tubal infertility is indicated only in selected situations. Surgery is not indicated in all cases of mechanical tubal infertility — in severe tubal damage, IVF is preferred. Active or recurrent inflammation is a contraindication to surgery as it worsens tubal damage and adhesion formation. Obstruction of one tube alone is generally not an indication for surgery if the other tube is patent and functional, as natural conception remains possible; surgery may be considered only if the blocked tube forms a hydrosalpinx or causes pain. The most appropriate indication is when conservative treatment fails and the patient strongly desires pregnancy. Common procedures include salpingolysis, fimbrioplasty, tuboplasty, and tubal recanalization.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: The following is characteristic for Stein–Leventhal syndrome: 1. Menstrual irregularities starting from menarche  2. Pathological hair growth 1.5–2 years after start of menstruation  3. Infertility  4. Normal development of mammary glands
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Stein–Leventhal syndrome (PCOS) is characterised by hyperandrogenism, chronic anovulation, and polycystic ovaries. Menstrual irregularities (oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea) starting from menarche are common due to chronic anovulation. Hirsutism (pathological hair growth) appears 1.5–2 years after menarche due to increased androgen levels. Infertility occurs from anovulation or irregular ovulation. Breast development is usually normal because oestrogen production is still present despite impaired ovulation. All four features are therefore characteristic of Stein–Leventhal syndrome.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: The reasons of female infertility are: a. Inflammatory diseases of genitals  b. Infantilism and hypoplasia of genitals  c. Total debilitating diseases and intoxication
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Female infertility can result from multiple factors. Inflammatory diseases (PID, salpingitis, endometritis) lead to tubal obstruction, adhesions, and impaired ovum transport. Infantilism and hypoplasia of the genital organs (underdeveloped uterus, ovaries, or tubes) prevent normal ovulation, implantation, or pregnancy maintenance — hypoplastic fallopian tubes are also long, thin, and tortuous, predisposing to ectopic pregnancy. General debilitating diseases (tuberculosis, diabetes, renal disease), severe malnutrition, and toxic exposures (tobacco, alcohol, drugs, chemicals) disturb hormonal balance and ovulation. All three are major categories of female infertility.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: Tubal infertility may be conditioned with: a. Sclerotic changes in the muscular wall of the uterine tube  b. Uterine tube reception abnormality  c. Infantilism
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: All three can cause tubal infertility. Sclerotic changes (fibrosis from chronic inflammation) impair tubal peristalsis and ovum transport. Uterine tube reception abnormality (impaired fimbrial function) prevents the ovum from entering the tube after ovulation. Infantilism — though often considered a uterine/endocrine cause — causes long, thin, narrow, and tortuous fallopian tubes with impaired peristalsis and ovum transport, predisposing to either infertility or ectopic pregnancy. All three mechanisms are therefore valid causes of tubal infertility.

Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.question: Factors conditioning tubal infertility during chronic salpingo-oophoritis are: 1. Stricture or obliteration of uterine tubes  2. Damage of ciliary epithelium of uterine tube mucous membrane  3. Development of peritubal commissures  4. Local hyperthermy
Reproductive Medicine & Infertility.explanation: Chronic salpingo-oophoritis leads to structural and functional tubal damage through three main mechanisms. Stricture or obliteration: chronic inflammation causes fibrosis and scarring, leading to narrowing or complete blockage of the tubes. Damage of ciliary epithelium: the ciliated epithelium normally moves the ovum toward the uterus — inflammation destroys these cilia, impairing ovum transport. Peritubal commissures (adhesions): inflammatory processes cause adhesions around the tubes, distorting their position and interfering with fimbrial ovum pickup. Local hyperthermy is not a primary mechanism of tubal infertility in chronic salpingo-oophoritis.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: As a rule, the cytogenic study of a complete hydatidiform mole displays:
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: A complete hydatidiform mole results from fertilization of an empty ovum (no maternal chromosomes) — all genetic material is paternal. Typically one sperm fertilizes the empty ovum and duplicates, giving 46XX karyotype (most common). 46XY can occur with dispermy but is less common. The mole is diploid (46 chromosomes), entirely paternal, with no fetal tissue.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: Prophylactic chemotherapy in patient with hydatidiform mole is indicated in: 1. In case of infection  2. Women with persisting and not regressing hCG level  3. Women with history of previous hydatidiform mole  4. High-risk group woman, refuses hysterectomy
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: Prophylactic chemotherapy for hydatidiform mole is indicated in: persistent/non-regressing β-hCG (indicates persistent trophoblastic disease), history of previous mole (high-risk group), and high-risk patients refusing hysterectomy (high-risk features: very high β-hCG, large uterus, theca lutein cysts, age >40). Infection alone is treated with antibiotics and is NOT an indication for chemotherapy.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: Hydatidiform mole which erodes the wall of the uterus is:
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: An aggressive (invasive) mole penetrates molar villi into the myometrium, eroding the uterine wall. It may cause uterine perforation and hemorrhage. β-hCG remains persistently elevated. Persistent mole refers to continued elevation of β-hCG but does not specifically imply myometrial invasion. Atrophic and perforative mole are not standard classifications.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: Surgery in case of choriocarcinoma is indicated in cases of: 1. Lung metastasis  2. Uterine perforation and haemorrhage  3. Large-size growth in the uterus  4. Ineffective chemotherapy
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: Choriocarcinoma is highly chemosensitive — chemotherapy is primary treatment. Surgery is reserved for: uterine perforation/haemorrhage (life-threatening, requires emergency intervention), large bulky uterine lesion (hysterectomy in selected cases, especially if family complete), and chemoresistant disease. Lung metastasis is treated with systemic chemotherapy, NOT surgery.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: The following complications can appear in hydatidiform mole: 1. Constipation  2. Thyroid storm  3. Uterine perforation  4. Haemorrhage
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: Complications of hydatidiform mole include: thyroid storm (β-hCG structural similarity to TSH stimulates thyroid — very high levels cause hyperthyroidism), uterine perforation (especially in invasive/aggressive mole with myometrial invasion), and haemorrhage (most common complication, from enlarged vascular uterus). Constipation is not a recognized complication.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: WHO classification of gestational trophoblastic disease is as follows: 1. Metastatic benign  2. Non-metastatic malignant  3. Metastatic malignant  4. Benign
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: WHO classifies GTD into: benign (complete and partial hydatidiform mole), non-metastatic malignant (GTN confined to uterus, persistent β-hCG), and metastatic malignant (invasive mole, choriocarcinoma with distant spread — most commonly lung). 'Metastatic benign' is NOT a recognized category — benign forms do not metastasize.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: The high-risk group of occurrence of hydatidiform mole is: 1. Women below the age of 20  2. Nulliparous women at age of 30  3. Multiparous women after menopause  4. Multiparous women of 40 and above
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: Hydatidiform mole has a bimodal age distribution: women <20 years (immature oocyte function) and women ≥40 years (markedly increased risk, further rises beyond 45). Nulliparous women at 30 and post-menopausal women are not established high-risk groups. Extremes of reproductive age are the key risk factor.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: Hydatidiform mole can be: 1. Complete  2. General  3. Partial  4. Obstructed
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: Hydatidiform mole is classified into complete mole (no fetal tissue, diploid 46XX, entirely paternal) and partial mole (some fetal tissue possible, triploid 69XXX/69XXY). 'General' and 'obstructed' are not recognized mole classifications.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: Preferable treatment for hydatidiform mole is:
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: The treatment of choice for hydatidiform mole is surgical evacuation — suction curettage (vacuum aspiration) followed by serial β-hCG monitoring. Hysterectomy may be considered in women >40 who have completed their family. Chemotherapy is reserved for persistent trophoblastic disease or rising β-hCG post-evacuation. Radiotherapy and laser have no role.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: All mentioned are trophoblastic diseases, EXCEPT:
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: Gestational trophoblastic diseases (GTD) arise from abnormal trophoblastic tissue and include: hydatidiform mole (benign GTD), persistent trophoblastic disease (malignant GTN — non-metastatic or metastatic), and choriocarcinoma (highly malignant, absent chorionic villi, early hematogenous spread). Adenocarcinoma is a malignant glandular epithelial tumor — completely unrelated to trophoblastic tissue.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: Malignant trophoblastic disease is:
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: Choriocarcinoma is a highly malignant trophoblastic tumor with absent chorionic villi, markedly elevated β-hCG, and early hematogenous spread to lungs, brain, and liver. Hydatidiform mole is generally benign GTD (may progress). Adenosarcoma is a malignant mixed mesenchymal tumor, and adenocarcinoma is a glandular epithelial malignancy — neither are trophoblastic.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: Patients with history of hydatidiform mole should be kept under observation for:
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: Post-molar follow-up requires serial β-hCG monitoring (weekly until normalization, then monthly) and effective contraception for 1 year to allow accurate β-hCG interpretation and detect persistent trophoblastic disease, invasive mole, or choriocarcinoma. A plateau or rise in β-hCG during this period indicates persistent disease requiring chemotherapy.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: In patients with hydatidiform mole, X-ray is essential to rule out:
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: The lungs are the most common site of metastasis in gestational trophoblastic disease, via hematogenous spread. Chest X-ray is therefore routinely performed in all patients with molar pregnancy. Brain metastasis can occur but is evaluated by CT/MRI in advanced cases. Kidney and stomach metastases are not typical.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: The necessary investigations in patients with hydatidiform mole are: 1. Ultrasound  2. Laparoscopy  3. X-ray  4. Serum beta-hCG levels
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: Essential investigations for hydatidiform mole: ultrasound (first-line, shows 'snowstorm' appearance, confirms absence of fetus in complete mole), chest X-ray (rule out pulmonary metastasis — most common metastatic site), and serum β-hCG (markedly elevated, used for diagnosis, treatment monitoring, and detecting persistent disease). Laparoscopy has no role in routine molar evaluation.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: All the following complications can appear in hydatidiform mole, EXCEPT:
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: Recognized complications of hydatidiform mole include: embolization (trophoblastic tissue entering circulation, pulmonary involvement), infection (retained molar tissue causing endometritis/sepsis), and hemorrhage (most common, from enlarged vascular uterus). Bowel perforation is NOT a complication — uterine perforation may occur in invasive mole, but bowel involvement is not typical.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: For the patient with uterine choriocarcinoma the availability of lutein cysts influences the outcome:
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: The presence of theca-lutein cysts in patients with uterine choriocarcinoma is associated with unfavourable prognosis. Lutein cysts develop due to excessive stimulation of the ovaries by very high levels of beta-hCG produced by the trophoblastic tumour. Their presence indicates high tumour activity, large tumour mass, and higher risk of metastasis. They are therefore considered a poor prognostic sign in gestational trophoblastic disease.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: Following methods are used in the diagnosis of trophoblastic disease: 1. Ultrasound  2. X-ray  3. Histological  4. Laboratory (detection of hCG)
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: All four methods are used in diagnosing gestational trophoblastic disease. Ultrasound: primary imaging method — in hydatidiform mole shows the snowstorm appearance with absence of a normal fetus in complete mole. X-ray: chest X-ray detects pulmonary metastases, common in malignant trophoblastic disease. Histological examination: of evacuated uterine tissue confirms the diagnosis and differentiates the specific type. Laboratory detection of beta-hCG: the most important laboratory test, used for diagnosis, monitoring treatment response, and detecting recurrence.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: Modern methods of treatment of patients with trophoblastic disease are: 1. Surgical  2. Chemotherapeutical  3. Radiation  4. Hormonal
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: Treatment of gestational trophoblastic disease mainly involves surgery and chemotherapy. Surgical treatment: suction evacuation of the uterus for hydatidiform mole, or hysterectomy in selected patients. Chemotherapy: main treatment for malignant trophoblastic disease — methotrexate and actinomycin-D. Radiotherapy is not a standard treatment. Hormonal therapy has no role in the treatment of trophoblastic tumours.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: The detection of which substance is most effective for trophoblastic disease diagnostics?
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: Beta-hCG (chorionic gonadotropin) is the key and most effective laboratory marker for trophoblastic disease — markedly elevated in hydatidiform mole and very high in choriocarcinoma. It is used for diagnosis, monitoring treatment response, and detecting recurrence. Trophoblastic beta-globulin is not routinely used or as sensitive as beta-hCG. Chorionic somatotropin (human placental lactogen) is produced by the placenta but is not useful for diagnosing trophoblastic tumours.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: The bilateral lutein cysts in case of hydatidiform mole require:
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: Bilateral theca-lutein cysts associated with hydatidiform mole usually regress spontaneously after evacuation of the mole as beta-hCG levels fall, therefore observation is recommended. Surgical intervention is required only if complications occur (torsion or rupture). Hormonal therapy has no role in the management of lutein cysts associated with trophoblastic disease.

Trophoblastic Disease.question: After a spontaneous abortion at 14 weeks a 34-year-old patient has had bleeding for 3 months. Twice she has undergone uterine cavity curettage but with no effect. She began also coughing. The most probable diagnosis is:
Trophoblastic Disease.explanation: The clinical presentation is classic for choriocarcinoma: history of a pregnancy event (spontaneous abortion at 14 weeks), persistent uterine bleeding for 3 months despite two curettages (curettage does not stop bleeding from choriocarcinoma), and new onset of cough (lung metastases — the most common metastatic site). The classic triad: persistent bleeding after pregnancy event, very high beta-hCG, and pulmonary symptoms from lung metastases. Placental polyp may cause persistent bleeding but usually improves after curettage and does not cause metastasis.

Diagnostic Methods.question: The indications of operative hysteroscopy are following: 1. Polypectomy  2. Hysterectomy  3. Endometrial ablation  4. Lysis of intrauterine adhesions
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Operative hysteroscopy is indicated for: polypectomy (direct visualization and resection of endometrial polyps), endometrial ablation (for dysfunctional uterine bleeding), and lysis of intrauterine adhesions/adhesiolysis (Asherman syndrome). Hysterectomy is performed abdominally, vaginally, or laparoscopically — it is NOT a hysteroscopic procedure.

Diagnostic Methods.question: Rectal examination is performed in: 1. Large myomas  2. Virgins  3. Carcinoma of cervix  4. Women with rectal symptoms
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Rectal examination is indicated in: virgins (to avoid vaginal examination while assessing uterus and adnexa), carcinoma cervix (essential for staging — assesses parametrial involvement, posterior extension, rectal invasion), and women with rectal symptoms. Large myomas are assessed by abdominal examination and bimanual palpation — rectal examination is not routinely required.

Diagnostic Methods.question: All listed are endoscopic methods of examination, EXCEPT:
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Endoscopic methods involve insertion of an optical instrument into a body cavity: laparoscopy (pelvic organs via abdominal wall), colposcopy (magnified cervical/vaginal visualization), and salpingoscopy (fallopian tube lumen). Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves — it is a radiological imaging method, not an endoscopic procedure.

Diagnostic Methods.question: Possible complications of laparoscopy: 1. Gas embolism  2. Inguinal hernia  3. Haemorrhage  4. Surgical emphysema
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Laparoscopy complications include: gas embolism (CO₂ enters venous circulation — rare but serious), haemorrhage (vascular/organ injury), and surgical emphysema (subcutaneous emphysema from CO₂ tracking into tissues). Inguinal hernia is NOT a typical complication; trocar-site incisional hernia can occur but is not inguinal hernia.

Diagnostic Methods.question: The laparoscopy is indicated in all cases, EXCEPT:
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Laparoscopy is indicated for tubal infertility (chromotubation, adhesiolysis), chronic pelvic pain (diagnose endometriosis/adhesions), and ovarian cysts (cystectomy, evaluation). Generalized peritonitis is a contraindication — severe infection, risk of spreading sepsis, and hemodynamic instability make laparotomy the appropriate approach.

Diagnostic Methods.question: Indications for diagnostic laparoscopy are: 1. Endometriosis  2. Generalized peritonitis  3. Chronic pelvic pain  4. PID
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Diagnostic laparoscopy is indicated for endometriosis (gold standard — direct visualization and biopsy), chronic pelvic pain (detects endometriosis, adhesions), and PID when diagnosis is uncertain or not responding to treatment. Generalized peritonitis is a contraindication requiring emergency laparotomy.

Diagnostic Methods.question: All mentioned are referred to the precancerous disease of cervix, EXCEPT:
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: CIN 2 (moderate dysplasia), CIS/carcinoma in situ (full-thickness dysplasia = CIN 3), and CIN 3 (severe dysplasia/HSIL) are all precancerous cervical lesions. VIN 2 (Vulvar Intraepithelial Neoplasia grade 2) is a precancerous lesion of the VULVA, not the cervix.

Diagnostic Methods.question: The indications of diagnostic hysteroscopy are following: 1. Lost intrauterine device  2. Evaluation of the endocervical canal  3. Ectopic pregnancy  4. Uterine synechiae
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Diagnostic hysteroscopy visualizes the uterine cavity and endocervical canal. Indications include: lost IUCD (locate and remove under direct vision), evaluation of endocervical canal (polyps, stenosis), and uterine synechiae/Asherman's syndrome (confirms adhesions, allows simultaneous adhesiolysis). Ectopic pregnancy is located outside the uterine cavity and is diagnosed by ultrasound and β-hCG — hysteroscopy has no role.

Diagnostic Methods.question: Intrauterine synechiae can be diagnosed by: 1. Hysteroscopy  2. Hysterosalpingography  3. Laparoscopy  4. Colposcopy
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Intrauterine synechiae (Asherman's syndrome) are diagnosed by: hysteroscopy (gold standard — direct visualization and simultaneous adhesiolysis) and HSG (shows irregular cavity, filling defects, obliteration). Laparoscopy evaluates external pelvic organs and does not visualize the uterine cavity. Colposcopy examines the cervix and vagina only.

Diagnostic Methods.question: The laparoscopy is contraindicated in all cases, EXCEPT:
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Tubal infertility is a major INDICATION for laparoscopy (chromotubation, adhesiolysis, endometriosis diagnosis). Extensive peritoneal adhesions (risk of bowel/vascular injury), intestinal obstruction (distended bowel, perforation risk), and haemodynamic instability (pneumoperitoneum increases intra-abdominal pressure, unsafe) are all contraindications.

Diagnostic Methods.question: Imaging techniques in gynecology are the following, EXCEPT:
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Imaging techniques produce visual representations of internal structures using radiological modalities: HSG (contrast X-ray of uterine cavity and tubes), plain X-ray, and CT scan. Hysteroscopy is an ENDOSCOPIC procedure — it uses direct optical visualization of the uterine cavity via an inserted instrument. It is classified as endoscopy, not imaging.

Diagnostic Methods.question: Endometrial biopsy is helpful:
options: As a screening test for carcinoma of the uterine corpus
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Endometrial biopsy is primarily used as a screening/diagnostic tool for endometrial carcinoma and hyperplasia, especially in women with abnormal uterine bleeding, postmenopausal bleeding, or high-risk features (obesity, anovulation). It is not used to diagnose infections (requires culture/swabs), not the primary tool for infertility (replaced by hormonal assays/USS), and does not directly assess ovarian function.

Diagnostic Methods.question: Difficult and painful coitus is called:
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Dyspareunia is defined as painful sexual intercourse. It may be superficial (introital — from vaginitis, vulvodynia) or deep (pelvic — from endometriosis, PID, pelvic adhesions). Dysphasia is a speech disorder. Dysuria is painful urination. Dystrophia refers to abnormal tissue development or degeneration.

Diagnostic Methods.question: Diagnostic methods often used in the primary reveal of benign tumours of women's genitals: 1. Gynaecological examination 2. Ultrasound investigation 3. X-Ray 4. All the mentioned
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Gynaecological examination (careful history and bimanual examination palpating the uterus for size, shape, mobility, and adnexal pathology — many asymptomatic fibroids are first detected at check-up) and ultrasound (the first-line and gold standard imaging modality for pelvic pathology — easy, cost-effective, and capable of revealing unsuspected pathology) are the primary tools. X-ray has a minor role in modern gynaecological practice and is not a standard primary method for detecting benign tumours, though incidentally it may show a calcified fibroid.

Diagnostic Methods.question: The followings are methods of treatment of patients suffering malignant tumours:
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Management of malignant tumours involves multiple treatment modalities. Surgery: often the primary treatment for many gynaecological malignancies. Radiotherapy: used as primary treatment, adjuvant therapy after surgery, or palliative treatment. Chemotherapy: for advanced or metastatic cancers, gestational trophoblastic tumours, and adjuvant therapy. Hormonal therapy: for hormone-sensitive tumours such as endometrial or breast cancer.

Diagnostic Methods.question: Malignant tumour of mucous tissue is:
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Carcinoma is a malignant tumour arising from epithelial tissue, which includes mucous membranes, glandular epithelium, and surface epithelium. Examples include cervical carcinoma, endometrial carcinoma, and gastric carcinoma. Leiomyoma is a benign tumour of smooth muscle tissue. Osteosarcoma is a malignant tumour of bone-forming tissue. Myosarcoma is a malignant tumour of muscle tissue, not epithelial tissue.

Diagnostic Methods.question: The malignant tumour from connective tissue is:
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Sarcoma is the general term for malignant tumours originating from connective (mesenchymal) tissue, including fibrous tissue, bone, cartilage, muscle, and fat. Examples include osteosarcoma, fibrosarcoma, liposarcoma, and leiomyosarcoma. Myosarcoma is a specific subtype of sarcoma arising from muscle tissue. Lymphosarcoma is a malignant tumour of lymphoid tissue. Fibrolipoma is a benign tumour of fibrous and adipose tissue.

Diagnostic Methods.question: In which age does breast cancer most often develop?
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Breast cancer incidence rises progressively with age and is most common after 60 years (postmenopausal women). Risk increases due to prolonged oestrogen exposure, accumulation of genetic mutations, and age-related hormonal changes. Breast cancer is rare in women younger than 30 years — most breast lesions in this age group are benign. Incidence begins to increase around perimenopause (45–50 years) but the peak frequency is after 60.

Diagnostic Methods.question: The breast cancer is, as a rule, a unilateral process. Is that right?
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: In most patients, breast cancer arises in a single breast (unilateral), usually developing in one quadrant — most commonly the upper outer quadrant. Bilateral breast cancer is relatively uncommon, occurring in approximately 2–5% of cases. Therefore breast cancer is, as a rule, a unilateral process.

Diagnostic Methods.question: Is only surgical treatment sufficient for the treatment of breast cancer?
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Breast cancer treatment requires a multimodal approach — surgery alone is not sufficient in most cases. Treatment typically combines surgery (lumpectomy or mastectomy), radiation therapy (commonly after breast-conserving surgery), chemotherapy (for locally advanced or high-risk disease), hormonal therapy (for hormone-receptor-positive tumours), and targeted therapy (for HER2-positive tumours). Because breast cancer may have microscopic systemic spread, surgery alone cannot eliminate all malignant cells.

Diagnostic Methods.question: The following is a benign tumour from angienchyma:
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Hemangioma is a benign tumour originating from blood vessels (vascular endothelium), representing a tumour of angiogenic tissue (angienchyma). It presents as a red or bluish vascular mass that is often soft and compressible. Lipoma is a benign tumour of adipose tissue. Glioma arises from glial cells of the nervous system. Adenoma is a benign tumour of glandular epithelium, not vascular tissue.

Diagnostic Methods.question: Benign tumour from muscular tissue is:
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Leiomyoma is a benign tumour originating from smooth muscle tissue, most commonly occurring in the uterus as uterine fibroids, composed of proliferating smooth muscle cells arranged in bundles. Glioma is a tumour of glial cells found in the central nervous system, not muscle tissue. Lipoma is a benign tumour of adipose tissue. Teratoma is a germ cell tumour containing tissues from multiple embryonic layers.

Diagnostic Methods.question: The most frequently occurring benign disease of the uterus is:
Diagnostic Methods.explanation: Fibromyoma (uterine leiomyoma) is the most common benign tumour of the uterus, arising from the smooth muscle cells of the myometrium. It is very common in women of reproductive age, presenting with menorrhagia, pelvic pressure, and reproductive problems. Endometriosis is not a tumour — it is a condition characterised by ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity. Cervical polyps are benign mucosal growths but are less common than uterine fibroids.

Endocrinology & Hormones.question: Hypothalamus produces the following hormones:
Endocrinology & Hormones.explanation: The hypothalamus produces releasing and inhibiting factors including GnRH (stimulates FSH/LH), TRH, CRH, and GHRH. GnRH is most important in gynecology, regulating ovarian function and menstrual cycle. Estrogens are from ovarian follicles, progesterone (gestagens) from corpus luteum/placenta, and corticosteroids from the adrenal cortex.

Endocrinology & Hormones.question: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) controls the synthesis and secretion of which substances?
Endocrinology & Hormones.explanation: GnRH is secreted by the hypothalamus in a pulsatile manner and acts on the anterior pituitary to stimulate synthesis and release of FSH and LH. FSH drives follicular growth and estrogen production; LH triggers ovulation and corpus luteum function. Norepinephrine and dopamine are neurotransmitters; prolactin is regulated by dopamine (inhibitory), not GnRH.

Endocrinology & Hormones.question: What hormones of the hypophysis (pituitary) take part in regulation of menstrual cycle? 1. LH  2. ACTH  3. TSH  4. FSH
Endocrinology & Hormones.explanation: The menstrual cycle is regulated by FSH (stimulates follicular growth and estrogen production) and LH (triggers ovulation and maintains corpus luteum) from the anterior pituitary via the HPO axis. ACTH regulates the adrenal cortex and TSH regulates the thyroid — neither directly regulates the menstrual cycle, though thyroid disorders can indirectly affect menstruation.

Endocrinology & Hormones.question: Last menstruation is considered the one from:
options: Last day of the last normal menstruation
First day of any bloody discharge
First day of the last normal menstruation
Last day of any bloody discharge
Endocrinology & Hormones.explanation: The Last Menstrual Period (LMP) is defined as the first day of the last normal menstrual bleeding. It is used to calculate gestational age and estimated date of delivery. The last day is not used. Abnormal spotting or irregular discharge does not qualify — it must be normal menstrual flow.

Endocrinology & Hormones.question: In the ovary the androgens serve as substrate for the formation of:
Endocrinology & Hormones.explanation: Two-cell, two-gonadotropin theory: LH stimulates theca cells to produce androgens (androstenedione, testosterone); FSH stimulates granulosa cells to aromatize these androgens into estrogens. Androgens are substrates ONLY for estrogen synthesis. Progesterone is synthesized from cholesterol via pregnenolone — a separate pathway not involving androgens.

Endocrinology & Hormones.question: Estrogens are secreted by:
Endocrinology & Hormones.explanation: Estrogens are produced by: granulosa cells of ovarian follicles (major source in reproductive age, via aromatization), corpus luteum (also secretes estrogens alongside progesterone in luteal phase), and adrenal cortex (produces androgens such as DHEA that are peripherally converted to estrogens). All three sources contribute.

Endocrinology & Hormones.question: The biosynthesis of the following takes place in the ovary: 1. Estrogens  2. Gestagens  3. Androgens  4. Oxytocin
Endocrinology & Hormones.explanation: The ovary synthesizes estrogens (granulosa cells via aromatase), gestagens/progesterone (corpus luteum after ovulation), and androgens (theca interna cells under LH). Oxytocin is synthesized in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary — it is NOT produced in the ovary.

Endocrinology & Hormones.question: FSH stimulates:
options: Growth of follicles in the ovary
Endocrinology & Hormones.explanation: FSH acts on ovarian granulosa cells to stimulate follicular growth and maturation, granulosa cell proliferation, and aromatase activity (converting androgens to estrogens). Corticosteroids are produced by the adrenal cortex under ACTH control. TTH/TSH is regulated by TRH, not FSH. Not all listed options are correct, so 'all mentioned' is wrong.

Endocrinology & Hormones.question: Characteristics of progesterone include all the following, EXCEPT:
options: It is an intermediary product in steroid metabolism
Its main source during early pregnancy is the corpus luteum of pregnancy
Its ovarian source is important after the first 12 weeks of pregnancy
Endocrinology & Hormones.explanation: Progesterone is a C21 steroid and an intermediate in steroid metabolism (cholesterol → pregnenolone → progesterone, serving as precursor to corticosteroids, androgens, and estrogens — all true). The corpus luteum is the main source in early pregnancy (true). After 10–12 weeks, the luteo-placental shift occurs and the placenta takes over progesterone production — the ovarian source becomes non-essential after this point.

PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.question: Polycystic ovarian syndrome is characterized by: 1. Hyperandrogenaemia 2. Low FSH/LH ratio 3. High FSH/LH ratio 4. Raised LH level
PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.explanation: PCOS is characterised by hyperandrogenaemia (raised testosterone, androstenedione, DHEA in ~50% of patients), raised LH level (excess inhibin stimulates LH and suppresses FSH), and a low FSH/LH ratio (LH is disproportionately high relative to FSH, so FSH/LH falls). A high FSH/LH ratio would imply the opposite of the PCOS hormonal profile.

PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.question: Woman with polycystic ovarian syndrome complains of: 1. Oligomenorrhea 2. Abdominal pain 3. Amenorrhea 4. Infertility
PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.explanation: PCOS classically presents with oligomenorrhoea (~87% of cases), amenorrhoea (~26% of cases), and anovulatory infertility (~20% of infertility cases). Abdominal pain is not a characteristic complaint; dysmenorrhoea is notably absent in PCOS. Occasional acute pain can occur if a cyst undergoes torsion or rupture, but chronic abdominal pain is not a standard feature.

PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.question: Polycystic ovarian syndrome is:
PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.explanation: PCOS is defined as a heterogeneous, multisystem endocrinopathy characterised by metabolic disturbances and a wide clinical spectrum including hyperandrogenism, raised LH, increased LH/FSH ratio, oligomenorrhoea, hirsutism, obesity, and infertility. While women with PCOS have increased risk of endometrial cancer due to unopposed oestrogen, the syndrome itself is an endocrinopathy.

PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.question: Much of the testosterone in polycystic ovarian syndrome is secreted by:
PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.explanation: Testosterone and androstenedione in PCOS are primarily secreted by the ovarian stromal cells (theca cells), stimulated by LH. In PCOS, insulin resistance and hyperinsulinaemia induce LH to cause thecal and stromal hyperplasia, leading to excess androgen secretion. Approximately 50% of total testosterone comes from the ovaries, specifically from the stromal tissue.

PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.question: Surgical treatment for polycystic ovarian syndrome is:
PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.explanation: The surgical treatment for PCOS when medical therapy fails is laparoscopic ovarian drilling — puncture of cysts (follicles) using cautery or laser. No more than 4 cysts should be punctured in each ovary to avoid adhesions or ovarian destruction. This improves response to hormonal ovulation stimulation and fertility rates. Endometrial ablation is for abnormal uterine bleeding; oophorectomy and hysterectomy are not indicated for PCOS itself.

PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.question: The infertility or subfertility during polycystic ovarian syndrome results from which of the following?
PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.explanation: Infertility in PCOS is directly due to anovulatory cycles. PCOS is a major cause of anovulatory infertility, accounting for approximately 20% of such cases. The endocrine disturbances (high LH, increased LH/FSH ratio) lead to non-ovulation. Hirsutism, obesity, and insulin resistance are features or contributing pathogenic factors of PCOS, but the direct mechanical cause of infertility is the failure to ovulate.

PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.question: Anovulation in women with polycystic ovarian syndrome is characterized by which of the following?
PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.explanation: PCOS is associated with inappropriate gonadotropin secretion — an increased LH/FSH ratio often exceeding 3:1. Excess inhibin causes low FSH but high LH, which is present even in the pre-ovulatory phase, preventing dominant follicle development and causing anovulation. FSH/LH ratio therefore falls (not rises). Hyperprolactinaemia is seen in ~15–20% of PCOS cases but is not the primary characterisation of anovulation.

PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.question: Which of the following leads to development of Sheehan's syndrome:
PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.explanation: Sheehan's syndrome is pituitary necrosis resulting from severe postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) and obstetric shock. Vascular thrombosis of the pituitary vessels causes panhypopituitarism. Clinical features include failure to lactate, lethargy, and signs of cortisol and thyroid deficiency.

PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.question: Which syndrome is characterized as a panhypopituitarism:
PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.explanation: Sheehan's syndrome is panhypopituitarism resulting from pituitary necrosis caused by vascular thrombosis after severe PPH. Chiari–Frommel is a hypopituitary state but not explicitly equated with panhypopituitarism. Turner's syndrome is hypergonadotropic hypogonadism due to 45 XO karyotype. Savage syndrome is gonadotropin-resistant ovary syndrome.

PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.question: Following are specific for Sheehan's syndrome: 1. Low blood sugar 2. High blood sugar 3. Low thyroid function 4. High thyroid function
PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.explanation: Sheehan's syndrome is panhypopituitarism from pituitary necrosis after severe PPH. It causes low blood sugar and low thyroid function (leading to lethargy) due to failure of pituitary hormone secretion. High blood sugar or high thyroid function are opposite findings and would suggest pituitary overactivity rather than failure.

PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.question: Sheehan's syndrome is:
PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.explanation: Sheehan's syndrome is secondary amenorrhoea because it occurs after childbirth — the woman has previously menstruated before the event causing pituitary necrosis. Primary amenorrhoea is the failure of menstruation to begin by age 16, which is inapplicable here. While Sheehan's is hypogonadotropic in its hormonal profile, it is classified as a pituitary cause of secondary amenorrhoea.

PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.question: Chiari–Frommel syndrome is a:
PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.explanation: Chiari–Frommel syndrome is listed under hypogonadotropic primary amenorrhoea, specifically as a pituitary cause alongside Simmond's disease and Forbes–Albright syndrome. It is characterised as a hypopituitary state with elevated prolactin.

PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.question: Savage syndrome (Gonadotropin-resistant ovaries) is a:
PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.explanation: Savage syndrome (gonadotropin-resistant ovary syndrome) is hypergonadotropic primary amenorrhoea. FSH levels are raised above 40 mIU/mL. The ovaries are histologically normal with primordial follicles, but granulosa cells fail to respond to FSH due to a receptor defect. It is classified under hypergonadotropic primary amenorrhoea in the standard classification.

PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.question: The diagnostic values of adrenogenital syndrome are: 1. High 17-hydroxyprogesterone 2. High 17-ketosteroids 3. Low 17-hydroxyprogesterone 4. Low 17-ketosteroids
PCOS & Adrenal/Hormonal Disorders.explanation: Adrenogenital syndrome (congenital adrenal hyperplasia) is diagnosed by elevated 17α-hydroxyprogesterone (very high values are diagnostic of 21-hydroxylase deficiency) and elevated 17-ketosteroids (values above 25 mg in 24 hours indicate adrenal hyperplasia; normal is 5–15 mg/24h).
